translated_text:
Section

As for the comprehensive conclusion, it contains useful principles.

The First Principle

Allah, glorified is He, is described through affirmation and negation. Affirmation includes His declaration that He knows all things, has power over all things, and is All-Hearing, All-Seeing, and other such descriptions. Negation includes His saying: “Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him.”

It should be understood that negation conveys neither praise nor perfection unless it entails affirmation. Mere negation, otherwise, conveys neither praise nor perfection, for pure negation is pure nonexistence. Pure nonexistence is nothing, and what is nothing is, as has been said, nothing—let alone a source of praise or perfection. Moreover, pure negation can describe both the nonexistent and the impossible, neither of which can be described as possessing anything praiseworthy or perfect.

For this reason, the descriptions by which Allah characterizes Himself through negation generally entail the affirmation of something praiseworthy, as in His saying:

“Allah—there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting Sustainer of all. Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him,”

through to His saying:

“And preserving them both does not weary Him.”

Negating drowsiness and sleep entails the perfection of His life and His self-subsistence and sustaining of all. It thus makes clear the perfection of His being the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting Sustainer of all. Likewise, His saying:

“And preserving them both does not weary Him”

means that it causes Him neither hardship nor burden. This entails the perfection and completeness of His power, unlike a created being who possesses power but can accomplish something only with effort and difficulty: this is a deficiency in his power and a defect in his strength. Likewise, His saying:

“Not an atom’s weight in the heavens or on earth escapes Him.”

Negating anything’s escaping Him entails His knowledge of every atom in the heavens and on earth. Likewise, His saying:

“We certainly created the heavens and the earth and everything between them in six days, and no weariness touched Us.”

Negating any touch of weariness—which means fatigue and exhaustion—indicates perfect power and utmost strength, unlike a created being, who is subject to fatigue and exhaustion. Likewise, His saying:

“Vision does not encompass Him.”

He negated only apprehension in the sense of encompassing Him, as most scholars have explained; He did not negate seeing Him as such. For what does not exist cannot be seen, and there is nothing praiseworthy in its not being seen. Were that so, what does not exist would be praiseworthy. Rather, what is praiseworthy is that He cannot be encompassed even when He is seen, just as He cannot be encompassed even when He is known. Thus, just as knowing Him does not mean encompassing Him in knowledge, seeing Him does not mean encompassing Him in vision.

original_text:
فَكَانَ فِي نَفْيِ الْإِدْرَاكِ مِنْ إثْبَاتِ عَظَمَتِهِ مَا يَكُونُ مَدْحًا وَصِفَةَ كَمَالٍ وَكَانَ ذَلِكَ دَلِيلًا عَلَى إثْبَاتِ الرُّؤْيَةِ لَا عَلَى نَفْيِهَا لَكِنَّهُ دَلِيلٌ عَلَى إثْبَاتِ الرُّؤْيَةِ مَعَ عَدَمِ الْإِحَاطَةِ وَهَذَا هُوَ الْحَقُّ الَّذِي اتَّفَقَ عَلَيْهِ سَلَفُ الْأُمَّةِ وَأَئِمَّتُهَا وَإِذَا تَأَمَّلْت ذَلِكَ:
 وَجَدْت كُلَّ نَفْيٍ لَا يَسْتَلْزِمُ ثُبُوتًا هُوَ مِمَّا لَمْ يَصِفْ اللَّهُ بِهِ نَفْسَهُ فَاَلَّذِينَ لَا يَصِفُونَهُ إلَّا بِالسُّلُوبِ: لَمْ يُثْبِتُوا فِي الْحَقِيقَةِ إلَهًا مَحْمُودًا بَلْ وَلَا مَوْجُودًا وَكَذَلِكَ مَنْ شَارَكَهُمْ فِي بَعْضِ ذَلِكَ كَاَلَّذِينَ قَالُوا لَا يَتَكَلَّمُ أَوْ لَا يَرَى أَوْ لَيْسَ فَوْقَ الْعَالَمِ أَوْ لَمْ يَسْتَوِ عَلَى الْعَرْشِ وَيَقُولُونَ: لَيْسَ بِدَاخِلِ الْعَالَمِ وَلَا خَارِجَهُ وَلَا مُبَايِنًا لِلْعَالَمِ وَلَا محايثا لَهُ؛ إذْ هَذِهِ الصِّفَاتُ يُمْكِنُ أَنْ يُوصَفَ بِهَا الْمَعْدُومُ؛ وَلَيْسَتْ هِيَ صِفَةً مُسْتَلْزِمَةً صِفَةَ ثُبُوتٍ وَلِهَذَا 
" قَالَ مَحْمُودُ بْنُ سبكتكين "
 لِمَنْ ادَّعَى ذَلِكَ فِي الْخَالِقِ: مَيِّزْ لَنَا بَيْنَ هَذَا الرَّبِّ الَّذِي تُثْبِتُهُ وَبَيْنَ الْمَعْدُومِ. وَكَذَلِكَ كَوْنُهُ لَا يَتَكَلَّمُ أَوْ لَا يَنْزِلُ لَيْسَ فِي ذَلِكَ صِفَةُ مَدْحٍ وَلَا كَمَالٍ؛
 بَلْ هَذِهِ الصِّفَاتُ فِيهَا تَشْبِيهٌ لَهُ بِالْمَنْقُوصَاتِ أَوْ الْمَعْدُومَاتِ فَهَذِهِ الصِّفَاتُ:
 مِنْهَا مَا لَا يَتَّصِفُ بِهِ إلَّا الْمَعْدُومُ وَمِنْهَا مَا لَا يَتَّصِفُ بِهِ إلَّا الْجَمَادَاتُ وَالنَّاقِصُ فَمَنْ قَالَ: لَا هُوَ مُبَايِنٌ لِلْعَالَمِ وَلَا مُدَاخِلٌ لِلْعَالَمِ فَهُوَ بِمَنْزِلَةِ مَنْ قَالَ: لَا هُوَ قَائِمٌ بِنَفْسِهِ وَلَا بِغَيْرِهِ وَلَا قَدِيمٌ وَلَا مُحْدَثٌ وَلَا مُتَقَدِّمٌ عَلَى الْعَالَمِ وَلَا مُقَارِنٌ لَهُ
translated_text:
Thus, negating encompassing Him affirms His greatness in a way that constitutes praise and an attribute of perfection. This is evidence affirming that He is seen, not denying it; rather, it affirms that He is seen without being encompassed. This is the truth upon which the early generations of the Muslim community and its leading scholars agreed. If you reflect on this, you will find that every negation that entails no affirmation is something with which Allah has not described Himself.

Those who describe Him only through negations have not, in reality, affirmed a praiseworthy deity—or even an existing one. The same applies to those who share some of their views, such as those who say that He does not speak, does not see, is not above the world, or did not rise over the Throne. They say that He is neither within the world nor outside it, neither separate from the world nor occupying the same place as it. These descriptions can apply to what does not exist, and they entail no affirmative attribute. For this reason, Mahmūd ibn Sabuktakīn said to someone who made such claims about the Creator: “Distinguish for us between this Lord whom you affirm and what does not exist.” Likewise, saying that He does not speak or does not descend contains no attribute of praise or perfection.

Rather, these descriptions liken Him to deficient or nonexistent things. Some of them apply only to what does not exist, while others apply only to inanimate or deficient things. Whoever says, “He is neither separate from the world nor within it,” is like someone who says, “He neither subsists by Himself nor through another; He is neither beginningless nor originated; and He neither precedes the world nor is contemporaneous with it.”

original_text:
وَمَنْ قَالَ:
 إنَّهُ لَيْسَ بِحَيِّ وَلَا مَيِّتٍ وَلَا سَمِيعٍ وَلَا بَصِيرٍ وَلَا مُتَكَلِّمٍ لَزِمَهُ أَنْ يَكُونَ مَيِّتًا أَصَمَّ أَعْمَى أَبْكَمَ.
 فَإِنْ قَالَ:
 الْعَمَى عَدَمُ الْبَصَرِ عَمَّا مَنْ شَأْنُهُ أَنْ يَقْبَلَ الْبَصَرَ وَمَا لَمْ يَقْبَلْ الْبَصَرَ كَالْحَائِطِ لَا يُقَالُ لَهُ أَعْمَى وَلَا بَصِيرٌ قِيلَ لَهُ: هَذَا اصْطِلَاحٌ اصْطَلَحْتُمُوهُ وَإِلَّا فَمَا يُوصَفُ بِعَدَمِ الْحَيَاةِ وَالسَّمْعِ وَالْبَصَرِ وَالْكَلَامِ: يُمْكِنُ وَصْفُهُ بِالْمَوْتِ وَالْعَمَى وَالْخَرَسِ وَالْعُجْمَةِ وَأَيْضًا فَكُلُّ مَوْجُودٍ يَقْبَلُ الِاتِّصَافَ بِهَذِهِ الْأُمُورِ وَنَقَائِضِهَا فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ قَادِرٌ عَلَى جَعْلِ الْجَمَادِ حَيًّا كَمَا جَعَلَ عَصَى مُوسَى حَيَّةً ابْتَلَعَتْ الْحِبَالَ وَالْعِصِيَّ وَأَيْضًا فَاَلَّذِي لَا يَقْبَلُ الِاتِّصَافَ بِهَذِهِ الصِّفَاتِ أَعْظَمُ نَقْصًا مِمَّنْ لَا يَقْبَلُ الِاتِّصَافَ بِهَا مَعَ اتِّصَافِهِ بِنَقَائِضِهَا.
 فَالْجَمَادُ الَّذِي لَا يُوصَفُ بِالْبَصَرِ وَلَا الْعَمَى وَلَا الْكَلَامِ وَلَا الْخَرَسِ:
 أَعْظَمُ نَقْصًا مِنْ الْحَيِّ الْأَعْمَى الْأَخْرَسِ فَإِذَا قِيلَ: إنَّ الْبَارِي لَا يُمْكِنُ اتِّصَافُهُ بِذَلِكَ: كَانَ فِي ذَلِكَ مِنْ وَصْفِهِ بِالنَّقْصِ أَعْظَمُ مِمَّا إذَا وُصِفَ بِالْخَرَسِ وَالْعَمَى وَالصَّمَمِ وَنَحْوَ ذَلِكَ؛ مَعَ أَنَّهُ إذَا جُعِلَ غَيْرَ قَابِلٍ لَهَا كَانَ تَشْبِيهًا لَهُ بِالْجَمَادِ الَّذِي لَا يَقْبَلُ الِاتِّصَافَ بِوَاحِدِ مِنْهَا. وَهَذَا تَشْبِيهٌ بِالْجَمَادَاتِ؛ لَا بِالْحَيَوَانَاتِ، فَكَيْفَ مَنْ قَالَ ذَلِكَ غَيْرُهُ مِمَّا يَزْعُمُ أَنَّهُ تَشْبِيهٌ بِالْحَيِّ
translated_text:
And whoever says, “He is neither living nor dead, nor does He hear, see, or speak,” must consequently regard Him as dead, deaf, blind, and mute.

If he says, “Blindness is the absence of sight in something capable by its nature of possessing sight; something incapable of sight, such as a wall, is called neither blind nor seeing,” he is answered: “This is a convention you have adopted. Otherwise, whatever is described as lacking life, hearing, sight, and speech can be described as possessing death, blindness, muteness, and inability to articulate speech. Moreover, everything that exists can possess these attributes and their opposites, for Allah is able to make inanimate things living, just as He turned Moses’ staff into a serpent that swallowed the ropes and staffs. Furthermore, that which cannot possess these attributes is more deficient than that which cannot possess them while possessing their opposites.”

An inanimate thing described as neither seeing nor blind, neither speaking nor mute, is more deficient than a living being that is blind and mute. Thus, to say that the Creator cannot possess these attributes is to ascribe a greater deficiency to Him than to describe Him as mute, blind, deaf, or the like. Moreover, to regard Him as incapable of possessing them is to liken Him to an inanimate thing incapable of possessing any of them. This likens Him to inanimate things, not to living creatures. How, then, can someone who says this [object to] others for what he claims amounts to likening Him to a living being?

original_text:
وَأَيْضًا فَنَفْسُ نَفْيِ هَذِهِ الصِّفَاتِ نَقْصٌ كَمَا أَنَّ إثْبَاتَهَا كَمَالٌ فَالْحَيَاةُ مِنْ حَيْثُ هِيَ هِيَ مَعَ قَطْعِ النَّظَرِ عَنْ تَعْيِينِ الْمَوْصُوفِ بِهَا صِفَةُ كَمَالٍ، وَكَذَلِكَ الْعِلْمُ وَالْقُدْرَةُ وَالسَّمْعُ وَالْبَصَرُ وَالْكَلَامُ وَالْفِعْلُ وَنَحْوُ ذَلِكَ؛
 وَمَا كَانَ صِفَةَ كَمَالٍ:
 فَهُوَ سُبْحَانَهُ أَحَقُّ أَنْ يَتَّصِفَ بِهِ مِنْ الْمَخْلُوقَاتِ فَلَوْ لَمْ يَتَّصِفْ بِهِ مَعَ اتِّصَافِ الْمَخْلُوقِ بِهِ: لَكَانَ الْمَخْلُوقُ أَكْمَلَ مِنْهُ.
وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّ الْجَهْمِيَّة الْمَحْضَةَ كَالْقَرَامِطَةِ وَمَنْ ضَاهَاهُمْ:
 يَنْفُونَ عَنْهُ تَعَالَى اتِّصَافَهُ بِالنَّقِيضَيْنِ حَتَّى يَقُولُونَ لَيْسَ بِمَوْجُودِ وَلَا لَيْسَ بِمَوْجُودِ وَلَا حَيٍّ وَلَا لَيْسَ بِحَيِّ وَمَعْلُومٌ أَنَّ الْخُلُوَّ عَنْ النَّقِيضَيْنِ مُمْتَنِعٌ فِي بَدَائِهِ الْعُقُولِ كَالْجَمْعِ بَيْنَ النَّقِيضَيْنِ. وَآخَرُونَ وَصَفُوهُ بِالنَّفْيِ فَقَطْ فَقَالُوا لَيْسَ بِحَيِّ وَلَا سَمِيعٍ وَلَا بَصِيرٍ؛ وَهَؤُلَاءِ أَعْظَمُ كُفْرًا مِنْ أُولَئِكَ مِنْ وَجْهٍ وَأُولَئِكَ أَعْظَمُ كُفْرًا مِنْ هَؤُلَاءِ مِنْ وَجْهٍ فَإِذَا قِيلَ لِهَؤُلَاءِ هَذَا مُسْتَلْزِمٌ وَصْفَهُ بِنَقِيضِ ذَلِكَ كَالْمَوْتِ وَالصَّمَمِ وَالْبُكْمِ قَالُوا إنَّمَا يَلْزَمُ ذَلِكَ لَوْ كَانَ قَابِلًا لِذَلِكَ وَهَذَا الِاعْتِذَارُ يَزِيدُ قَوْلَهُمْ فَسَادًا وَكَذَلِكَ مَنْ ضَاهَى هَؤُلَاءِ -
 وَهُمْ الَّذِينَ يَقُولُونَ:
 لَيْسَ بِدَاخِلِ الْعَالَمِ وَلَا خَارِجَهُ إذَا قِيلَ هَذَا مُمْتَنِعٌ فِي ضَرُورَةِ الْعَقْلِ كَمَا إذَا قِيلَ: لَيْسَ بِقَدِيمِ وَلَا مُحْدَثٍ - وَلَا وَاجِبٍ وَلَا مُمْكِنٍ وَلَا قَائِمٍ بِنَفْسِهِ وَلَا قَائِمٍ بِغَيْرِهِ قَالُوا هَذَا إنَّمَا يَكُونُ إذَا كَانَ قَابِلًا لِذَلِكَ وَالْقَبُولُ إنَّمَا يَكُونُ مِنْ الْمُتَحَيِّزِ فَإِذَا انْتَفَى التَّحَيُّزُ انْتَفَى قَبُولُ هَذَيْنِ الْمُتَنَاقِضَيْنِ.
translated_text:
Moreover, the very negation of these attributes is a deficiency, just as their affirmation is a perfection. Life, considered in itself and without regard to the particular being possessing it, is an attribute of perfection. The same is true of knowledge, power, hearing, sight, speech, action, and similar attributes. Whatever constitutes an attribute of perfection, He—glory be to Him—is more deserving of possessing it than created beings. If He did not possess it while a created being did, that created being would be more perfect than He.

Know that the thoroughgoing Jahmiyyah, such as the Qarmatians and those who resemble them, deny that He, the Exalted, possesses either of two contradictory attributes. They even say, “He is neither existent nor non-existent, neither living nor not living.” Yet it is self-evident to reason that possessing neither of two contradictories is impossible, just as possessing both is impossible.

Others describe Him solely in terms of negation, saying, “He is neither living, nor hearing, nor seeing.” These are greater in disbelief than the former in one respect, while the former are greater in disbelief than these in another. When these people are told, “This entails describing Him with the contradictory attributes, such as death, deafness, and muteness,” they reply, “That would follow only if He were capable of possessing such attributes.” This defense only makes their position more unsound.

The same applies to those who resemble them—namely, those who say, “He is neither within the world nor outside it.” When they are told, “This is self-evidently impossible to reason, just as it would be to say that He is neither eternal nor originated, neither necessary nor contingent, neither self-subsisting nor subsisting in another,” they reply, “This holds only if He is capable of such attributes. Such capability belongs only to what has spatial location. Thus, if spatial location is absent, so too is the capacity to possess either of these two contradictories.”

original_text:
فَيُقَالُ لَهُمْ عِلْمُ الْخَلْقِ بِامْتِنَاعِ الْخُلُوِّ مِنْهُ هَذَيْنِ النَّقِيضَيْنِ:
 هُوَ عِلْمٌ مُطْلَقٌ لَا يُسْتَثْنَى مِنْهُ مَوْجُودٌ وَالتَّحَيُّزُ الْمَذْكُورُ: إنْ أُرِيدَ بِهِ كَوْنُ الأحياز الْمَوْجُودَةِ تُحِيطُ بِهِ فَهَذَا هُوَ الدَّاخِلُ فِي الْعَالَمِ؛ وَإِنْ أُرِيدَ بِهِ أَنَّهُ مُنْحَازٌ عَنْ الْمَخْلُوقَاتِ؛ أَيْ مُبَايِنٌ لَهَا مُتَمَيِّزٌ عَنْهَا فَهَذَا هُوَ الْخُرُوجُ فَالْمُتَحَيِّزُ يُرَادُ بِهِ تَارَةً مَا هُوَ دَاخِلُ الْعَالَمِ وَتَارَةً مَا هُوَ خَارِجُ الْعَالَمِ فَإِذَا قِيلَ لَيْسَ بِمُتَحَيِّزِ كَانَ مَعْنَاهُ لَيْسَ بِدَاخِلِ الْعَالَمِ وَلَا خَارِجَهُ، فَهُمْ غَيَّرُوا الْعِبَارَةَ لِيُوهِمُوا مَنْ لَا يَفْهَمُ حَقِيقَةَ قَوْلِهِمْ أَنَّ هَذَا مَعْنًى آخَرَ وَهُوَ الْمَعْنَى الَّذِي عُلِمَ فَسَادُهُ بِضَرُورَةِ الْعَقْلِ؛ كَمَا فَعَلَ أُولَئِكَ بِقَوْلِهِمْ لَيْسَ بِحَيِّ وَلَا مَيِّتٍ وَلَا مَوْجُودٍ وَلَا مَعْدُومٍ وَلَا عَالِمٍ وَلَا جَاهِلٍ.
translated_text:
They are therefore told: Created beings’ knowledge that it is impossible for anything to lack both of these contradictories is universal; no existing being is exempt from it. As for the “spatial location” mentioned: if it means that existing regions of space encompass Him, then this means being within the world. If it means that He is separate from created beings—that is, distinct from them and apart from them—then this means being outside the world.

Thus, “what has spatial location” sometimes refers to what is within the world and sometimes to what is outside it. To say, “He has no spatial location,” therefore means that He is neither within the world nor outside it. They have changed the wording to mislead those who do not understand the true meaning of their statement into thinking that this is a different meaning. Yet it is the very meaning whose invalidity is self-evident to reason, just as those others did when they said, “He is neither living nor dead, neither existent nor non-existent, neither knowing nor ignorant.”

original_text:
الْقَاعِدَةُ الثَّانِيَةُ:
أَنَّ مَا أَخْبَرَ بِهِ الرَّسُولُ عَنْ رَبِّهِ فَإِنَّهُ يَجِبُ الْإِيمَانُ بِهِ - سَوَاءٌ عَرَفْنَا مَعْنَاهُ أَوْ لَمْ نَعْرِفْ - لِأَنَّهُ الصَّادِقُ الْمَصْدُوقُ؛
 فَمَا جَاءَ فِي الْكِتَابِ وَالسُّنَّةِ وَجَبَ عَلَى كُلِّ مُؤْمِنٍ الْإِيمَانُ بِهِ وَإِنْ لَمْ يَفْهَمْ مَعْنَاهُ وَكَذَلِكَ مَا ثَبَتَ بِاتِّفَاقِ سَلَفِ الْأُمَّةِ وَأَئِمَّتِهَا مَعَ أَنَّ هَذَا الْبَابَ يُوجَدُ عَامَّتُهُ مَنْصُوصًا فِي الْكِتَابِ وَالسُّنَّةِ مُتَّفَقٌ عَلَيْهِ بَيْنَ سَلَفِ الْأُمَّةِ وَمَا تَنَازَعَ فِيهِ الْمُتَأَخِّرُونَ نَفْيًا وَإِثْبَاتًا فَلَيْسَ عَلَى أَحَدٍ بَلْ وَلَا لَهُ:
 أَنْ يُوَافِقَ أَحَدًا عَلَى إثْبَاتِ لَفْظِهِ أَوْ نَفْيِهِ حَتَّى يَعْرِفَ مُرَادَهُ فَإِنْ أَرَادَ حَقًّا قُبِلَ وَإِنْ أَرَادَ بَاطِلًا رُدَّ وَإِنْ اشْتَمَلَ كَلَامُهُ عَلَى حَقٍّ وَبَاطِلٍ لَمْ يُقْبَلْ مُطْلَقًا وَلَمْ يُرِدْ جَمِيعَ مَعْنَاهُ بَلْ يُوقَفُ اللَّفْظُ وَيُفَسَّرُ الْمَعْنَى كَمَا تَنَازَعَ النَّاسُ فِي الْجِهَةِ وَالتَّحَيُّزِ وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ، فَلَفْظُ الْجِهَةِ قَدْ يُرَادُ بِهِ شَيْءٌ مَوْجُودٌ غَيْرُ اللَّهِ فَيَكُونُ مَخْلُوقًا كَمَا إذَا أُرِيدَ بِالْجِهَةِ نَفْسُ الْعَرْشِ أَوْ نَفْسُ السَّمَوَاتِ وَقَدْ يُرَادُ بِهِ مَا لَيْسَ بِمَوْجُودِ غَيْرِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى كَمَا إذَا أُرِيدَ بِالْجِهَةِ مَا فَوْقَ الْعَالَمِ وَمَعْلُومٌ أَنَّهُ لَيْسَ فِي النَّصِّ إثْبَاتُ لَفْظِ الْجِهَةِ وَلَا نَفْيُهُ كَمَا فِيهِ إثْبَاتُ الْعُلُوِّ وَالِاسْتِوَاءِ وَالْفَوْقِيَّةِ وَالْعُرُوجِ إلَيْهِ وَنَحْوُ ذَلِكَ وَقَدْ عُلِمَ أَنَّ مَا ثَمَّ مَوْجُودٌ
translated_text:
The Second Principle:

Whatever the Messenger has reported about his Lord must be believed—whether we understand its meaning or not—for he is truthful and confirmed in his truthfulness.

Every believer must therefore believe whatever is stated in the Quran and Sunnah, even if he does not understand its meaning. The same applies to what has been established by the agreement of the early generations of the Muslim community and its leading scholars. Indeed, most matters in this subject are explicitly stated in the Quran and Sunnah and agreed upon by the early generations of the Muslim community.

As for expressions whose affirmation or negation has been disputed by later scholars, no one is obliged—or even permitted—to agree with anyone in affirming or denying his expression until he understands what that person intends. If he intends something true, it is accepted; if he intends something false, it is rejected. If his statement contains both truth and falsehood, it should neither be accepted without qualification nor have its entire meaning rejected. Rather, judgment on the expression should be suspended and its meaning clarified. This applies, for example, to people’s disputes over direction, spatial location, and similar matters.

The word “direction” may mean an existing entity other than Allah, in which case it is created—as when “direction” means the Throne itself or the heavens themselves. It may also mean what is not an existing entity other than Allah Most High—as when “direction” means what is above the world.

It is well known that the revealed texts neither affirm nor deny the word “direction,” whereas they do affirm His being on high, His rising over the Throne, His being above, ascent to Him, and the like. It is also known that there is no existing being

إلَّا الْخَالِقَ وَالْمَخْلُوقَ وَالْخَالِقُ مُبَايِنٌ لِلْمَخْلُوقِ - سُبْحَانَهُ وَتَعَالَى - لَيْسَ فِي مَخْلُوقَاتِهِ شَيْءٌ مِنْ ذَاتِهِ؛ وَلَا فِي ذَاتِهِ شَيْءٌ مِنْ مَخْلُوقَاتِهِ.

 أَتُرِيدُ بِالْجِهَةِ أَنَّهَا شَيْءٌ مَوْجُودٌ مَخْلُوقٌ؟ فَاَللَّهُ لَيْسَ دَاخِلًا فِي الْمَخْلُوقَاتِ أَمْ تُرِيدُ بِالْجِهَةِ مَا وَرَاءَ الْعَالَمِ؟

 .

 وَفِي حَدِيثٍ آخَرَ: 
{وَإِنَّهُ لَيَدْحُوهَا كَمَا يَدْحُو الصِّبْيَانَ بِالْكُرَةِ}
 وَفِي حَدِيثِ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ: 
{مَا السَّمَوَاتُ السَّبْعُ وَالْأَرْضُونَ السَّبْعُ وَمَا فِيهِنَّ فِي يَدِ الرَّحْمَنِ إلَّا كَخَرْدَلَةِ فِي يَدِ أَحَدِكُمْ}
 وَإِنْ أَرَادَ بِهِ أَنَّهُ مُنْحَازٌ عَنْ الْمَخْلُوقَاتِ؛
 أَيْ مُبَايِنٌ لَهَا مُنْفَصِلٌ عَنْهَا لَيْسَ حَالًّا فِيهَا:
 فَهُوَ سُبْحَانَهُ كَمَا قَالَ أَئِمَّةُ السُّنَّةِ: فَوْقَ سَمَوَاتِهِ عَلَى عَرْشِهِ بَائِنٌ مِنْ خَلْقِهِ.
translated_text:
except the Creator and created beings. The Creator—glorified and exalted is He—is distinct from His creation. Nothing of His essence is within His creation, and nothing of His creation is within His essence.

Someone who denies direction should therefore be asked: Do you mean by “direction” an existing, created thing? Allah is not within created things. Or do you mean by “direction” what lies beyond the world? There is no doubt that Allah is above the world, distinct from created beings.

Likewise, someone who says that Allah is in a direction should be asked: Do you mean that Allah is above the world, or that Allah is within some created thing? If you mean the former, it is true; if you mean the latter, it is false.

The same applies to the expression “spatial location.” If someone means by it that created things contain Allah, then Allah is far greater and mightier than that. Indeed, His Kursī encompasses the heavens and the earth. Allah Most High has said:

“They have not esteemed Allah as He deserves. The whole earth will be in His grasp on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be rolled up in His right hand.”

It is established in the collections of authentic hadith that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah will grasp the earth and roll up the heavens in His right hand. Then He will say: ‘I am the King! Where are the kings of the earth?’”

In another hadith:

“Indeed, He tosses it as children toss a ball.”

And in the hadith of Ibn ‘Abbās:

“The seven heavens, the seven earths, and all that they contain are, in the Hand of the Most Merciful, no more than a mustard seed in the hand of one of you.”

If, however, someone means by it that He is separate from created beings—that is, distinct from them, apart from them, and not dwelling within them—then He, glorified is He, is as the imams of the Sunnah have said: above His heavens, upon His Throne, distinct from His creation.

الْقَاعِدَةُ الثَّالِثَةُ:
إذَا قَالَ الْقَائِلُ:
 ظَاهِرُ النُّصُوصِ مُرَادٌ أَوْ ظَاهِرُهَا لَيْسَ بِمُرَادِ فَإِنَّهُ يُقَالُ: لَفْظُ الظَّاهِرِ فِيهِ إجْمَالٌ وَاشْتِرَاكٌ فَإِنْ كَانَ الْقَائِلُ يَعْتَقِدُ أَنَّ ظَاهِرَهَا التَّمْثِيلُ بِصِفَاتِ الْمَخْلُوقِينَ أَوْ مَا هُوَ مِنْ خَصَائِصِهِمْ فَلَا رَيْبَ أَنَّ هَذَا غَيْرُ مُرَادٍ؛
 وَلَكِنَّ السَّلَفَ وَالْأَئِمَّةَ لَمْ يَكُونُوا يُسَمُّونَ هَذَا ظَاهِرَهَا وَلَا يَرْتَضُونَ أَنْ يَكُونَ ظَاهِرُ الْقُرْآنِ وَالْحَدِيثِ كُفْرًا وَبَاطِلًا وَاَللَّهُ سُبْحَانَهُ وَتَعَالَى أَعْلَمُ وَأَحْكَمُ مِنْ أَنْ يَكُونَ كَلَامُهُ الَّذِي وَصَفَ بِهِ نَفْسَهُ لَا يَظْهَرُ مِنْهُ إلَّا مَا هُوَ كُفْرٌ أَوْ ضَلَالٌ وَاَلَّذِينَ يَجْعَلُونَ ظَاهِرَهَا ذَلِكَ يَغْلَطُونَ مِنْ وَجْهَيْنِ:
 تَارَةً يَجْعَلُونَ الْمَعْنَى الْفَاسِدَ ظَاهِرَ اللَّفْظِ حَتَّى يَجْعَلُوهُ مُحْتَاجًا إلَى تَأْوِيلٍ يُخَالِفُ الظَّاهِرَ وَلَا يَكُونُ كَذَلِكَ،
 وَتَارَةً يَرُدُّونَ الْمَعْنَى الْحَقَّ الَّذِي هُوَ ظَاهِرُ اللَّفْظِ لِاعْتِقَادِهِمْ أَنَّهُ بَاطِلٌ (فَالْأَوَّلُ كَمَا قَالُوا فِي قَوْلِهِ:
 
{عَبْدِي جُعْت فَلَمْ تُطْعِمْنِي}
 الْحَدِيثَ وَفِي الْأَثَرِ الْآخَرِ: 
{الْحَجَرُ الْأَسْوَدُ يَمِينُ اللَّهِ فِي الْأَرْضِ فَمَنْ صَافَحَهُ أَوْ قَبَّلَهُ فَكَأَنَّمَا صَافَحَ اللَّهَ وَقَبَّلَ يَمِينَهُ}
 وَقَوْلِهِ: 
{قُلُوبُ الْعِبَادِ بَيْنَ أُصْبُعَيْنِ مِنْ أَصَابِعِ الرَّحْمَنِ}
 فَقَالُوا: قَدْ عُلِمَ أَنْ لَيْسَ فِي قُلُوبِنَا أَصَابِعُ الْحَقِّ
translated_text:
The Third Principle

If someone says, “The apparent meaning of the texts is intended,” or, “Their apparent meaning is not intended,” the response is: The term “apparent meaning” is ambiguous and has more than one sense. If the speaker believes that their apparent meaning likens Allah’s attributes to those of created beings, or ascribes to Him qualities peculiar to them, then there is no doubt that this is not intended.

However, the early generations and the imams did not call this their apparent meaning, nor would they accept that the apparent meaning of the Quran and hadith is disbelief and falsehood. Allah, glorified and exalted is He, is far too knowing and wise for His words describing Himself to have no apparent meaning other than disbelief or misguidance. Those who regard this as their apparent meaning err in two ways:

Sometimes they make an unsound meaning the apparent meaning of the wording, thereby treating it as requiring an interpretation contrary to its apparent meaning, when that is not the case. At other times, they reject the true meaning—which is the apparent meaning of the wording—because they believe it to be false.

(The first error is exemplified by what they say concerning His words:

“My servant, I was hungry, yet you did not feed Me,”

and the rest of the hadith; and concerning the other report:

“The Black Stone is Allah’s right hand on earth. Whoever shakes hands with it or kisses it is as though he had shaken hands with Allah and kissed His right hand.”

And His words:

“The hearts of the servants are between two fingers of the Most Merciful.”

They say: “It is known that the fingers of the True One are not within our hearts.”

translated_text:
So they should be told:

If you gave due consideration to what the texts signify, you would know that they indicate nothing but the truth. As for (the first example, the statement:

“The Black Stone is Allah’s right hand on earth. Whoever shakes hands with it and kisses it is as though he had shaken hands with Allah and kissed His right hand.”

This explicitly indicates that the Black Stone is neither an attribute of Allah nor His actual right hand, for it says:

“Allah’s right hand on earth,”

and:

“Whoever kisses it and shakes hands with it is as though he had shaken hands with Allah and kissed His right hand.”

It is well known that the thing being compared is not the thing to which it is compared. Thus, the report itself makes clear that whoever touches the Stone is not shaking hands with Allah, and that the Stone is not His actual right hand. How, then, can its apparent meaning be deemed disbelief on the grounds that it requires reinterpretation—especially when this report is known only from Ibn Abbās?

As for the other hadith, it appears in the Sahīh with its meaning explained:

“Allah says, ‘My servant, I was hungry, yet you did not feed Me.’ The servant replies, ‘My Lord, how could I feed You when You are the Lord of all worlds?’ He says, ‘Did you not know that My servant so-and-so was hungry? Had you fed him, you would have found that with Me. My servant, I was ill, yet you did not visit Me.’ The servant replies, ‘My Lord, how could I visit You when You are the Lord of all worlds?’ He says, ‘Did you not know that My servant so-and-so was ill? Had you visited him, you would have found Me with him.’”

This explicitly indicates that Allah, glorified is He, was neither ill nor hungry; rather, His servant was ill and His servant was hungry. He described His servant’s hunger as His own hunger and his illness as His own illness, explaining this with the words, “Had you fed him, you would have found that with Me,” and, “Had you visited him, you would have found Me with him.” Thus, no expression in the hadith remains that requires reinterpretation.

As for his statement:

“The hearts of the servants are between two fingers of the Most Merciful,”

its apparent meaning does not indicate that the heart is connected to the fingers, touches them, or contains them within it. Nor does someone’s saying, “This is between my two hands,” imply that it is in direct contact with his hands. Likewise, saying, “The clouds held in service between heaven and earth,” does not imply that they touch heaven and earth. There are many similar examples.

A similar kind of claim is to treat an expression as equivalent to another that is not equivalent to it. Thus, concerning His words:

“What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My two hands?”

it has been said that they are equivalent to His words:

“Have they not seen that We created for them livestock from what Our hands have made?”

Yet these two expressions are not equivalent. In the latter, He attributes the action to the hands, making it similar to His words:

“Because of what your hands have earned.”

In the former, however, He attributes the action to Himself, saying:

“What I created,”

and then:

“With My two hands.”

Furthermore, in this passage He refers to His holy Self in the singular, while using the dual form for the two hands, as in His words:

“Rather, both His hands are outstretched.”

In the other passage, He attributes the hands to Himself using the plural pronoun, making it comparable to His words:

“Sailing under Our eyes.”

This use of the (plural is analogous to His words:

“In His hand is the dominion,”

and “In His hand is all good,” in the (singular. Allah, glorified and exalted is He, sometimes refers to Himself in the singular, whether by an explicit noun or a pronoun, and sometimes in the plural, as in His words:

“Indeed, We have granted you a clear victory,”

and other similar passages. He never refers to Himself in the dual, for the plural form conveys the magnification that He deserves, and may also signify the meanings of His names.

As for the dual form, it indicates a limited number, and He is exalted above that. Thus, if He said:

“What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My two hands?”

this would not be equivalent to His words:

“From what Our hands have made.”

This is analogous to His words:

“In His hand is the dominion,”

and “In His hand is all good.” Even if He said, “I created,” using the singular form, it would differ from the other expression; how much more so when He says, “I created with My two hands,” using the dual form?

Alongside this is the evidence of the widely transmitted—indeed, mass-transmitted—hadiths, and the consensus of the early generations on what the Quran indicates, as explained at length elsewhere. One example is his statement:

“Those who act justly will be with Allah on pulpits of light, to the right of the Most Merciful—and both His hands are right hands: those who are just in their judgments, with their families, and in whatever is entrusted to them.”

There are other similar examples.

If the speaker believes that the apparent meaning of the texts whose meaning is disputed is of the same kind as the apparent meaning of those whose meaning is agreed upon—with the apparent meaning being intended in all of them—then, when Allah declared that He knows all things and has power over all things, and Ahl al-Sunnah and the leading scholars of the Muslims agreed that these statements are to be understood according to their apparent meaning and that this meaning is intended, it was understood that they did not mean that His knowledge is like our knowledge or His power like our power.

Likewise, when they agreed that He is truly living, truly knowing, and truly powerful, they did not mean that He is like a created being who possesses life, knowledge, and power. Similarly, when they say that His words, exalted is He:

“He loves them, and they love Him,”

“Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him,”

and:

“Then He rose over the Throne,”

are to be understood according to their apparent meaning, this does not imply that their apparent meaning entails a rising like that of a created being, love like its love, or pleasure like its pleasure.

translated_text:
If the listener supposes that the apparent meaning of the attributes is that they resemble the attributes of created beings, he must conclude that none of that apparent meaning is intended. But if he believes that their apparent meaning is what befits the Creator and is proper to Him, he cannot deny this apparent meaning or deny that it is intended without evidence supporting that denial.

Neither reason nor revelation provides any basis for denying this except grounds of the same kind as those used to deny the other attributes. Thus, the same argument applies to them all. To explain: some of our attributes are concrete entities and bodies that are parts of us, such as the face and hand. Others are qualities and accidents that inhere in us, such as hearing, sight, speech, knowledge, and power.

It is well known that when the Lord described Himself as living, knowing, and powerful, the Muslims did not declare this apparent meaning unintended on the grounds that what it signifies in His case is the same as what it signifies in ours. Likewise, when He described Himself as having created Adam with His two hands, this did not require declaring its apparent meaning unintended on the grounds that what it signifies in His case is like what it signifies in ours. Rather, an attribute befits the one who possesses it. Since His holy essence is not like the essences of created beings, His attributes, like His essence, are not like their attributes. The relation of a created being’s attribute to that being corresponds to the relation of the Creator’s attribute to Him; yet the attribute in one case is not like the attribute in the other, nor is the one to whom it belongs like the other.

As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“You will see your Lord as you see the sun and the moon.”

He thus likened the act of seeing to the act of seeing; he did not liken the One seen to the things seen.

translated_text:
This is clarified by:

The Fourth Principle

Many people imagine that some, many, most, or all of Allah’s attributes resemble the attributes of created beings. They then seek to deny what they have understood, thereby falling into four pitfalls:

First: They have likened what they understood from the texts to the attributes of created beings and assumed that the texts signify such a likeness.

Second: If they take this to be the meaning of the texts and reject it, the texts are left stripped of what they signify: the affirmation of attributes befitting Allah. Thus, besides their offense against the texts and their ill opinion of Allah and His Messenger—since they suppose that their words convey this false likeness—they have negated what Allah and His Messenger placed in their words: the affirmation of Allah’s attributes and the divine meanings befitting the majesty of Allah Most High.

Third: They deny these attributes of Allah—Mighty and Majestic—without knowledge, thereby denying the Lord what rightfully belongs to Him.

translated_text:
Fourth: He describes the Lord by the opposites of these attributes: the attributes of the dead and of inanimate things, or those of nonexistent things. He thereby denies the attributes of perfection that rightfully belong to the Lord, likens Him to deficient and nonexistent things, strips the texts of the attributes they signify, and makes their meaning out to be a likeness to created beings. Thus, in his treatment of Allah’s words and of Allah Himself, he combines denial of the divine attributes with likening Allah to creation, deviating concerning Allah’s names and signs.

An example is that all the texts indicate that Allah is exalted above created beings and that He rises over the Throne. His being above and distinct from created beings is known through reason in agreement with revelation; His rising over the Throne, however, is known through revelation.

Neither the Quran nor the Sunnah describes Him as neither within the world nor outside it, neither distinct from it nor intermingled with it. Yet someone under this misconception supposes that, if Allah is described as rising over the Throne, His doing so must resemble a person’s mounting ships and livestock, as in His words:

“and has made for you ships and livestock that you ride”

“so that you may settle upon their backs”.

He therefore imagines that, if Allah is over the Throne, He must need it just as someone riding a ship or an animal needs it: if the ship sank, its rider would fall, and if the animal stumbled, its rider would tumble down.

By this analogy, if the Throne ceased to exist, the Lord—glorified and exalted is He—would fall. Then, imagining that he is refuting this, he says: “His rising over the Throne is neither sitting nor settling.”

translated_text:
and it is not recognized that what is said of the meaning of rising over also applies to the meanings of sitting and settling. If dependence is included in those meanings, then there is no difference between rising over, sitting, and settling: in this sense, He is neither rising over, nor settled, nor sitting. If, however, their meanings include nothing beyond what is included in the meaning of rising over, then affirming one while denying the other is arbitrary. It is known that there are familiar distinctions between the meanings of rising over, settling, and sitting. The point here, however, is to recognize the error of someone who denies something while affirming its counterpart.

This error appears to stem from his mistaken understanding of Allah’s rising over the Throne: he supposes that it resembles a person’s mounting the backs of livestock or boarding ships. Yet nothing in this wording indicates that, for Allah attributes rising over to His noble Self, just as He attributes all His other acts and attributes to Himself. Thus, He states that He created and then rose over the Throne, just as He states that He determined and then guided, that He built the heaven with might, and that He is with Moses and Aaron, hearing and seeing, and other such things.

He does not speak of rising over in an unrestricted sense applicable to a created being, nor in a general sense encompassing created beings, just as He does not speak in such terms concerning His other attributes. Rather, He speaks of rising over as something He attributes to His noble Self. If it were supposed—on the basis of an impossible hypothesis—that He was like His creation—exalted is He above that—then His rising over would resemble that of His creation. But if He is not like His creation—indeed, it is known that He has no need of creation, that He is the Creator of the Throne and everything else, and that everything other than Him depends upon Him,

translated_text:
and He has no need of anything other than Himself, and He has spoken only of a rising over that is particular to Him, not one that applies to others and is unbefitting Him—just as, regarding His knowledge, power, sight, hearing, and creation, He speaks only of what is particular to Him—then how can anyone imagine that, if He is risen over the Throne, He needs it, and that, if the Throne were to fall, the One above it would fall down? Glorified and exalted is He, far above what the wrongdoers and deniers say! Is this anything but sheer ignorance and error on the part of anyone who understands or imagines such a thing, supposes it to be the apparent meaning and import of the wording, or considers it possible for the Lord of all worlds, who has no need of creation? Rather, even if an ignorant person were supposed to understand or imagine something like this, it should be explained to him that this is impossible and that the wording does not indicate it at all, just as it does not indicate comparable notions in any of the other attributes with which the Lord describes Himself.

When He, glorified and exalted, says:

“And the heaven We constructed with strength,”

can anyone imagine that His building resembles that of a human being in need, who requires a basket, shovels, the making of bricks, the preparation of clay, and helpers?

Moreover, it is known that Allah Most High created the world with some of its parts above others, without making its higher parts dependent upon its lower ones. The air is above the earth, yet does not need the earth to support it. The clouds, too, are above the earth, yet do not need it to support them. The heavens are above the earth, yet do not need the earth to support them. Thus, the Most High, the Highest, the Lord of all things

translated_text:
and their Sovereign—if He is above all His creation, how could it follow that He needs His creation or His Throne? How could His being above His creation entail such dependence when it does not entail this even among created things? It is known that whatever independence from others is established for a created being, the Creator, glorified and exalted, has a greater and more rightful claim to it. The same applies to His words:

“Do you feel secure that He who is in heaven will not cause the earth to swallow you, whereupon it would quake?”

Anyone who imagines that this verse implies that Allah is inside the heavens is, by agreement, ignorant and astray—even though saying that the sun and moon are in the sky does imply that they are within it. For the preposition “in” is connected to what precedes and follows it, and its meaning varies according to what it is related to. Thus, a distinction is made between a thing being in a place, a body being in a region of space, an accident being in a body, a face being in a mirror, and speech being on paper. Each of these kinds has a distinctive feature that sets it apart from the others, although the preposition “in” is used in all of them.

If someone were to ask, “Is the Throne in heaven or on earth?” the answer would be, “In heaven.” Likewise, if someone asked, “Is Paradise in heaven or on earth?” the answer would be, “Paradise is in heaven.” Yet this does not entail that the Throne is inside the heavens, nor even that Paradise is. It is established in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When you ask Allah for Paradise, ask Him for al-Firdaws, for it is the highest and central part of Paradise, and its roof is the Throne of the Most Merciful.”

Thus, the roof of this Paradise—the Throne—is above the celestial spheres, even though Paradise is in

heaven, where the term denotes what is above, whether Paradise is above the celestial spheres or below them. Allah Most High says:

“Let him stretch a rope up to the ceiling.”

And He says:

“And We sent down from the sky purifying water.”

Since it was firmly established in the minds of those addressed that Allah is the Most High, the Highest, and that He is above everything, His saying that He is in heaven was understood to mean that He is above, and above everything. Likewise, when he asked the slave girl, “Where is Allah?” and she replied, “In heaven,” she meant only that He is above, not that He is confined to created bodies or dwells within them.

The expression “above” includes what is above all created things. Thus, whatever is above them all is “in heaven.” This does not imply that an actually existing enclosure surrounds Him, for nothing exists above the world except Allah. Similarly, saying that the Throne is in heaven does not imply that the Throne is inside some other existing, created thing.

If, however, “heaven” is taken to mean the celestial spheres, the meaning would be that He is above them, just as He says:

“And I will surely crucify you on the trunks of palm trees.”

And:

“Travel through the land.”

And:

“Journey through the land.”

Likewise, one may say that someone is “in the mountain” or “on the roof,” even when he is on its highest part.

The Fifth Principle:
We know what we have been told in one respect, but not in another.

For Allah says:

“Do they not reflect upon the Quran? Had it been from anyone other than Allah, they would have found in it much inconsistency.”

And He says:

“Have they not reflected upon the Word?”

And He says:

“This is a blessed Book which We have sent down to you, so that they may reflect upon its verses and those of understanding may take heed.”

And He says:

“Do they not reflect upon the Quran, or are there locks upon their hearts?”

Thus, He commands reflection upon the entire Book. Allah Most High also says:

“He is the One who has sent down to you the Book. In it are clear verses, which are the foundation of the Book, and others that are not entirely clear. Those whose hearts are inclined to deviation follow what is not entirely clear in it, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation. But none knows its interpretation except Allah. Those firmly grounded in knowledge say, ‘We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord.’ And none take heed except those of understanding.”

The majority of the early and later generations of the Muslim community hold that the pause comes at His words:

“But none knows its interpretation except Allah.”

This is what has been transmitted from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, and others.

وَرُوِيَ عَنْ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 التَّفْسِيرُ عَلَى أَرْبَعَةِ أَوْجُهٍ تَفْسِيرٌ تَعْرِفُهُ الْعَرَبُ مِنْ كَلَامِهَا وَتَفْسِيرٌ لَا يُعْذَرُ أَحَدٌ بِجَهَالَتِهِ وَتَفْسِيرٌ تَعْلَمُهُ الْعُلَمَاءُ وَتَفْسِيرٌ لَا يَعْلَمُهُ إلَّا اللَّهُ مَنْ ادَّعَى عِلْمَهُ فَهُوَ كَاذِبٌ وَقَدْ رُوِيَ عَنْ مُجَاهِدٍ وَطَائِفَةٍ: أَنَّ الرَّاسِخِينَ فِي الْعِلْمِ يَعْلَمُونَ تَأْوِيلَهُ وَقَدْ قَالَ مُجَاهِدٌ: عَرَضْت الْمُصْحَفَ عَلَى ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ مِنْ فَاتِحَتِهِ إلَى خَاتِمَتِهِ أُوقِفُهُ عِنْدَ كُلِّ آيَةٍ وَأَسْأَلُهُ عَنْ تَفْسِيرِهَا وَلَا مُنَافَاةَ بَيْنَ الْقَوْلَيْنِ عِنْدَ التَّحْقِيقِ فَإِنَّ لَفْظَ التَّأْوِيلِ قَدْ صَارَ بِتَعَدُّدِ الِاصْطِلَاحَاتِ مُسْتَعْمَلًا فِي ثَلَاثَةِ مَعَانٍ:
أَحَدُهَا:
 وَهُوَ اصْطِلَاحُ كَثِيرٍ مِنْ الْمُتَأَخِّرِينَ مِنْ الْمُتَكَلِّمِينَ فِي الْفِقْهِ وَأُصُولِهِ: أَنَّ التَّأْوِيلَ هُوَ صَرْفُ اللَّفْظِ عَنْ الِاحْتِمَالِ الرَّاجِحِ إلَى الِاحْتِمَالِ الْمَرْجُوحِ؛ لِدَلِيلِ يَقْتَرِنُ بِهِ وَهَذَا هُوَ الَّذِي عَنَاهُ أَكْثَرُ مَنْ تَكَلَّمَ مِنْ الْمُتَأَخِّرِينَ فِي تَأْوِيلِ نُصُوصِ الصِّفَاتِ وَتَرْكِ تَأْوِيلِهَا؛ وَهَلْ ذَلِكَ مَحْمُودٌ أَوْ مَذْمُومٌ أَوْ حَقٌّ أَوْ بَاطِلٌ؟ .
الثَّانِي:
 أَنَّ التَّأْوِيلَ بِمَعْنَى التَّفْسِيرِ وَهَذَا هُوَ الْغَالِبُ عَلَى اصْطِلَاحِ الْمُفَسِّرِينَ لِلْقُرْآنِ كَمَا يَقُولُ ابْنُ جَرِيرٍ وَأَمْثَالُهُ - مِنْ الْمُصَنِّفِينَ فِي التَّفْسِيرِ - وَاخْتَلَفَ عُلَمَاءُ التَّأْوِيلِ وَمُجَاهِدٌ إمَامُ الْمُفَسِّرِينَ؛
 قَالَ الثَّوْرِيُّ:
 
" إذَا جَاءَك التَّفْسِيرُ عَنْ مُجَاهِدٍ فَحَسْبُك بِهِ "
 وَعَلَى تَفْسِيرِهِ يَعْتَمِدُ الشَّافِعِيُّ وَأَحْمَدُ وَالْبُخَارِيُّ وَغَيْرُهُمَا فَإِذَا ذَكَرَ أَنَّهُ يَعْلَمُ تَأْوِيلَ الْمُتَشَابِهِ فَالْمُرَادُ بِهِ مَعْرِفَةُ تَفْسِيرِهِ.
translated_text:
and it is reported that Ibn ‘Abbās said:

“Explanation of the Quran is of four kinds: an explanation that the Arabs know from their language; an explanation that no one is excused for not knowing; an explanation known to scholars; and an explanation known only to Allah. Whoever claims to know the last is a liar.”

It has also been reported from Mujāhid and others that those firmly grounded in knowledge know its interpretation. Mujāhid said:

“I went through the Quran with Ibn ‘Abbās from beginning to end, stopping him at every verse and asking him about its explanation.”

On careful examination, there is no contradiction between the two views, for differing terminological conventions have resulted in the term ta’wīl (interpretation) being used in three senses:

The first:

In the terminology of many later scholars discussing jurisprudence and its principles, ta’wīl means taking an expression in its less likely sense rather than its more likely sense, on the basis of accompanying evidence. This is what most later scholars meant when discussing whether to apply ta’wīl to the texts concerning Allah’s attributes or refrain from doing so, and whether this is praiseworthy or blameworthy, true or false.

The second:

Ta’wīl means explanation. This is its predominant usage among Quranic commentators, as when Ibn Jarīr and other authors of Quranic commentaries say, “The scholars of interpretation differed.” Mujāhid is a leading authority among Quranic commentators. Al-Thawrī said:

“If an explanation comes to you from Mujāhid, that is sufficient for you.”

Al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad, al-Bukhārī, and others rely upon his explanations. Thus, when he states that he knows the ta’wīl of what is not entirely clear, he means knowing its explanation.

The third meaning of ta’wīl:

It is the reality to which the words ultimately refer, as Allah Most High says:

“Do they await anything but its fulfillment? On the Day its fulfillment comes, those who had forgotten it before will say, ‘The messengers of our Lord certainly brought the truth.’”

Thus, the ta’wīl of the Quran’s accounts of the Hereafter is what Allah has foretold in it will come to pass: the Resurrection, the reckoning, recompense, Paradise, Hell, and the like. Likewise, Allah Most High relates in the account of Joseph that, when his parents and brothers prostrated before him, he said:

“O my father, this is the fulfillment of my earlier dream.”

He thus identified the very event that actually took place as the ta’wīl of the dream. The second meaning is the explanation of speech: the words used to explain an expression so that its meaning may be understood, or its rationale or supporting evidence known. This third meaning of ta’wīl, however, is the very thing that exists in reality.

An example is the statement of ‘Ā’ishah:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say while bowing and prostrating: ‘Glory and praise be to You, O Allah, our Lord. O Allah, forgive me.’”

He was putting the Quran into practice, meaning His words:

“So glorify your Lord with praise and seek His forgiveness.”

Another example is the statement of Sufyān ibn ‘Uyaynah: “The Sunnah is the ta’wīl of commands and prohibitions.” The commanded act itself is the ta’wīl of the command to perform it, and the actual thing about which a statement is made is the ta’wīl of that statement. Speech consists of statements and commands. This is why Abū ‘Ubayd and others say, “Jurists are more knowledgeable about ta’wīl than language scholars,” as

ذَكَرُوا ذَلِكَ فِي تَفْسِيرِ اشْتِمَالِ الصَّمَّاءِ؛ لِأَنَّ الْفُقَهَاءَ يَعْلَمُونَ تَفْسِيرَ مَا أَمَرَ بِهِ وَنَهَى عَنْهُ؛ لِعِلْمِهِمْ بِمَقَاصِدِ الرَّسُولِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ كَمَا يَعْلَمُ أَتْبَاعُ بقراط وَسِيبَوَيْهِ وَنَحْوِهِمَا مِنْ مَقَاصِدِهِمَا مَا لَا يُعْلَمُ بِمُجَرَّدِ اللُّغَةِ؛ وَلَكِنَّ تَأْوِيلَ الْأَمْرِ وَالنَّهْيِ لَا بُدَّ مِنْ مَعْرِفَتِهِ بِخِلَافِ تَأْوِيلِ الْخَبَرِ.
 إذَا عُرِفَ ذَلِكَ:
 فَتَأْوِيلُ مَا أَخْبَرَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى بِهِ عَنْ نَفْسِهِ الْمُقَدَّسَةِ الْمُتَّصِفَةِ بِمَا لَهَا مِنْ حَقَائِقِ الْأَسْمَاءِ وَالصِّفَاتِ هُوَ حَقِيقَةٌ لِنَفْسِهِ الْمُقَدَّسَةِ الْمُتَّصِفَةِ بِمَا لَهَا مِنْ حَقَائِقِ الصِّفَاتِ وَتَأْوِيلِ مَا أَخْبَرَ اللَّهُ بِهِ تَعَالَى مِنْ الْوَعْدِ وَالْوَعِيدِ هُوَ نَفْسُ مَا يَكُونُ مِنْ الْوَعْدِ وَالْوَعِيدِ وَلِهَذَا مَا يَجِيءُ فِي الْحَدِيثِ نَعْمَلُ بِمُحْكَمِهِ وَنُؤْمِنُ بِمُتَشَابِهِهِ لِأَنَّ مَا أَخْبَرَ اللَّهُ بِهِ عَنْ نَفْسِهِ وَعَنْ الْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ فِيهِ أَلْفَاظٌ مُتَشَابِهَةٌ يُشْبِهُ مَعَانِيهَا مَا نَعْلَمُهُ فِي الدُّنْيَا كَمَا أَخْبَرَ أَنَّ فِي الْجَنَّةِ لَحْمًا وَلَبَنًا وَعَسَلًا وَخَمْرًا وَنَحْوَ ذَلِكَ وَهَذَا يُشْبِهُ مَا فِي الدُّنْيَا لَفْظًا وَمَعْنًى؛ وَلَكِنْ لَيْسَ هُوَ مِثْلَهُ وَلَا حَقِيقَتَهُ فَأَسْمَاءُ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى وَصِفَاتُهُ أَوْلَى وَإِنْ كَانَ بَيْنَهُمَا وَبَيْنَ أَسْمَاءِ الْعِبَادِ وَصِفَاتِهِمْ تَشَابُهٌ أَنْ لَا يَكُونَ لِأَجْلِهَا الْخَالِقُ مِثْلَ الْمَخْلُوقِ، وَلَا حَقِيقَتُهُ كَحَقِيقَتِهِ وَالْإِخْبَارُ عَنْ الْغَائِبِ لَا يُفْهَمُ إنْ لَمْ يُعَبَّرْ عَنْهُ بِالْأَسْمَاءِ الْمَعْلُومَةِ مَعَانِيهَا فِي الشَّاهِدِ وَيُعْلَمُ بِهَا مَا فِي الْغَائِبِ بِوَاسِطَةِ الْعِلْمِ بِمَا فِي الشَّاهِدِ؛ مَعَ الْعِلْمِ بِالْفَارِقِ الْمُمَيِّزِ وَأَنَّ مَا أَخْبَرَ اللَّهُ بِهِ مِنْ الْغَيْبِ أَعْظَمُ مِمَّا يُعْلَمُ فِي الشَّاهِدِ وَفِي الْغَائِبِ
translated_text:
they mention when explaining ishtimāl al-sammā’ (a particular manner of wrapping oneself in a garment). For jurists understand what the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded and prohibited because they know his purposes, just as the followers of Hippocrates, Sībawayh, and others like them understand aspects of their purposes that cannot be known through language alone. Yet the ta’wīl of commands and prohibitions must be known, unlike the ta’wīl of statements.

Once this is understood, the ta’wīl of what Allah Most High has related about His holy Self, characterized by the realities of His names and attributes, is the actual reality of His holy Self, characterized by the realities of His attributes. The ta’wīl of what Allah Most High has related concerning promises and threats is the very fulfillment of those promises and threats. Hence the words found in the hadith:

“We act upon its clear passages and believe in its equivocal passages.”

For what Allah has related about Himself and the Last Day includes expressions whose meanings resemble what we know in this world. He has told us, for example, that Paradise contains meat, milk, honey, wine, and other such things. These resemble what exists in this world in wording and meaning, but they are neither identical to them nor the same in their actual reality. This applies all the more to Allah’s names and attributes: although they bear some resemblance to the names and attributes of His servants, that resemblance does not make the Creator like the created being, nor His reality like its reality.

An account of what is unseen cannot be understood unless it is expressed using names whose meanings are known in the observable world. Through these names, what is unseen is understood by means of our knowledge of what is observable, while recognizing the distinction between them and knowing that what Allah has related of the unseen is greater than what is known in the observable world. مَا لَا عَيْنٌ رَأَتْ وَلَا أُذُنٌ سَمِعَتْ وَلَا خَطَرَ عَلَى قَلْبِ بَشَرٍ فَنَحْنُ إذَا أَخْبَرَنَا اللَّهُ بِالْغَيْبِ الَّذِي اخْتَصَّ بِهِ:
 مِنْ الْجَنَّةِ وَالنَّارِ عَلِمْنَا مَعْنَى ذَلِكَ وَفَهِمْنَا مَا أُرِيدَ مِنَّا فَهْمُهُ بِذَلِكَ الْخِطَابِ وَفَسَّرْنَا ذَلِكَ وَأَمَّا نَفْسُ الْحَقِيقَةِ الْمُخْبَرِ عَنْهَا مِثْلَ الَّتِي لَمْ تَكُنْ بَعْدُ؛ وَإِنَّمَا تَكُونُ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ فَذَلِكَ مِنْ التَّأْوِيلِ الَّذِي لَا يَعْلَمُهُ إلَّا اللَّهُ وَلِهَذَا لَمَّا سُئِلَ مَالِكٌ وَغَيْرُهُ مِنْ السَّلَفِ عَنْ قَوْله تَعَالَى 
{الرَّحْمَنُ عَلَى الْعَرْشِ اسْتَوَى}
 قَالُوا: الِاسْتِوَاءُ مَعْلُومٌ وَالْكَيْفُ مَجْهُولٌ وَالْإِيمَانُ بِهِ وَاجِبٌ وَالسُّؤَالُ عَنْهُ بِدْعَةٌ،
 وَكَذَلِكَ قَالَ رَبِيعَةُ شَيْخُ مَالِكٍ قَبْلَهُ:
 الِاسْتِوَاءُ مَعْلُومٌ وَالْكَيْفُ مَجْهُولٌ وَمِنْ اللَّهِ الْبَيَانُ وَعَلَى الرَّسُولِ الْبَلَاغُ وَعَلَيْنَا الْإِيمَانُ فَبَيَّنَ أَنَّ الِاسْتِوَاءَ مَعْلُومٌ وَأَنَّ كَيْفِيَّةَ ذَلِكَ مَجْهُولٌ، وَمِثْلُ هَذَا يُوجَدُ كَثِيرًا فِي كَلَامِ السَّلَفِ، وَالْأَئِمَّةُ يَنْفُونَ عِلْمَ الْعِبَادِ بِكَيْفِيَّةِ صِفَاتِ اللَّهِ وَأَنَّهُ لَا يَعْلَمُ كَيْفَ اللَّهُ إلَّا اللَّهُ فَلَا يَعْلَمُ مَا هُوَ إلَّا هُوَ،
 وَقَدْ قَالَ النَّبِيُّ:
 
{لَا أُحْصِي ثَنَاءً عَلَيْك أَنْتَ كَمَا أَثْنَيْت عَلَى نَفْسِك}
 وَهَذَا فِي صَحِيحِ مُسْلِمٍ وَغَيْرِهِ وَقَالَ فِي الْحَدِيثِ الْآخَرِ: 
{اللَّهُمَّ إنِّي أَسْأَلُك بِكُلِّ اسْمٍ هُوَ لَك سَمَّيْت بِهِ نَفْسَكَ أَوْ أَنْزَلْته فِي كِتَابِك أَوْ عَلَّمْته أَحَدًا مَنْ خَلْقِك أَوْ اسْتَأْثَرْت بِهِ فِي عِلْمِ الْغَيْبِ عِنْدَك}
 وَهَذَا الْحَدِيثُ فِي الْمُسْنَدِ، وَصَحِيحِ أَبِي حَاتِمٍ وَقَدْ أَخْبَرَ فِيهِ أَنَّ لِلَّهِ مِنْ الْأَسْمَاءِ مَا اسْتَأْثَرَ بِهِ فِي عِلْمِ الْغَيْبِ عِنْدَهُ.

what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has ever conceived. Thus, when Allah tells us about matters of the unseen whose knowledge He has reserved to Himself—Paradise and Hell—we understand their meaning, grasp what we are intended to understand from that address, and explain it. But the actual reality described—such as that which has not yet come to pass and will come to pass only on the Day of Resurrection—belongs to the ta’wīl known only to Allah.

Hence, when Mālik and others among the early generations were asked about the Most High’s words:

“The Most Merciful rose over the Throne,”

they said: “Istiwā’ (rising over the Throne) is known; its manner is unknown. Belief in it is obligatory, and asking about it is an innovation.”

Likewise, Rabī‘ah, Mālik’s teacher, had said before him: “Istiwā’ is known; its manner is unknown. Explanation comes from Allah, conveying the message is the Messenger’s duty, and belief is our duty.” He thus made clear that istiwā’ is known, while its manner is unknown. Statements like this occur frequently in the words of the early generations. The imams deny that Allah’s servants know the manner of His attributes: none but Allah knows how He is, and none but He knows His true reality.

The Prophet said:

“I cannot fully praise You; You are as You have praised Yourself.”

This is recorded in Sahīh Muslim and elsewhere. In another hadith, he said:

“O Allah, I ask You by every name belonging to You with which You have named Yourself, or which You have revealed in Your Book, or taught to any of Your creation, or reserved to Yourself in Your knowledge of the unseen.”

This hadith is recorded in al-Musnad and Sahīh Abī Hātim. In it, he stated that Allah has names which He has reserved to Himself in His knowledge of the unseen.

فَمَعَانِي هَذِهِ الْأَسْمَاءِ الَّتِي اسْتَأْثَرَ بِهَا فِي عِلْمِ الْغَيْبِ عِنْدَهُ لَا يَعْلَمُهَا غَيْرُهُ. وَاَللَّهُ سُبْحَانَهُ أَخْبَرَنَا أَنَّهُ عَلِيمٌ قَدِيرٌ سَمِيعٌ بَصِيرٌ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ؛ إلَى غَيْرِ ذَلِكَ مِنْ أَسْمَائِهِ وَصِفَاتِهِ. فَنَحْنُ نَفْهَمُ مَعْنَى ذَلِكَ وَنُمَيِّزُ بَيْنَ الْعِلْمِ وَالْقُدْرَةِ وَبَيْنَ الرَّحْمَةِ وَالسَّمْعِ وَالْبَصَرِ، وَنَعْلَمُ أَنَّ الْأَسْمَاءَ كُلَّهَا اتَّفَقَتْ فِي دَلَالَتِهَا عَلَى ذَاتِ اللَّهِ مَعَ تَنَوُّعِ مَعَانِيهَا فَهِيَ مُتَّفِقَةٌ مُتَوَاطِئَةٌ مِنْ حَيْثُ الذَّاتُ مُتَبَايِنَةٌ مِنْ جِهَةِ الصِّفَاتِ وَكَذَلِكَ أَسْمَاءُ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ مِثْلُ مُحَمَّدٍ وَأَحْمَدَ وَالْمَاحِي وَالْحَاشِرِ وَالْعَاقِبِ. وَكَذَلِكَ أَسْمَاءُ الْقُرْآنِ مِثْلُ الْقُرْآنِ وَالْفُرْقَانِ وَالْهُدَى وَالنُّورِ وَالتَّنْزِيلِ وَالشِّفَاءِ وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ وَمِثْلُ هَذِهِ الْأَسْمَاءِ تَنَازَعَ النَّاسُ فِيهَا هَلْ هِيَ مِنْ قَبِيلِ الْمُتَرَادِفَةِ - لِاتِّحَادِ الذَّاتِ - أَوْ مِنْ قَبِيلِ الْمُتَبَايِنَةِ لِتَعَدُّدِ الصِّفَاتِ؟
 كَمَا إذَا قِيلَ:
 السَّيْفُ وَالصَّارِمُ وَالْمُهَنَّدُ وَقُصِدَ بِالصَّارِمِ مَعْنَى الصَّرْمِ وَفِي الْمُهَنَّدِ النِّسْبَةُ إلَى الْهِنْدِ؛ وَالتَّحْقِيقُ أَنَّهَا مُتَرَادِفَةٌ فِي الذَّاتِ مُتَبَايِنَةٌ فِي الصِّفَاتِ وَمِمَّا يُوَضِّحُ هَذَا أَنَّ اللَّهَ وَصَفَ الْقُرْآنَ كُلَّهُ بِأَنَّهُ مُحْكَمٌ وَبِأَنَّهُ مُتَشَابِهٌ وَفِي مَوْضِعٍ آخَرَ جَعَلَ مِنْهُ مَا هُوَ مُحْكَمٌ وَمِنْهُ مَا هُوَ مُتَشَابِهٌ فَيَنْبَغِي أَنْ يُعْرَفَ الْإِحْكَامُ وَالتَّشَابُهُ الَّذِي يَعُمُّهُ؛ وَالْإِحْكَامُ وَالتَّشَابُهُ الَّذِي يَخُصُّ بَعْضَهُ قَالَ
translated_text:
Thus, no one but He knows the meanings of those names which He has reserved to Himself in His knowledge of the unseen. Allah, glorified is He, has informed us that He is All-Knowing, All-Powerful, All-Hearing, All-Seeing, All-Forgiving, and Merciful, along with His other names and attributes. We understand what these mean and distinguish knowledge from power, and mercy from hearing and sight. We know that all these names refer to Allah’s essence, despite their different meanings. They agree and coincide in referring to His essence, while differing in the attributes they signify.

The same applies to the names of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, such as Muhammad, Ahmad, al-Māhī, al-Hāshir, and al-ʿĀqib. Likewise, the names of the Quran include the Quran, the Criterion, the Guidance, the Light, the Revelation, the Healing, and others. People have disputed whether names of this kind are synonymous because they refer to a single entity, or distinct because they signify different attributes.

An example is the use of al-sayf (the sword), al-sārim (the cutting blade), and al-muhannad (the Indian blade), when al-sārim is intended to convey the meaning of cutting, and al-muhannad a connection to India. The precise conclusion is that they are synonymous with respect to the entity they name, but distinct with respect to its attributes.

What further clarifies this is that Allah has described the entire Quran as perfectly formed and as mutually consistent, while elsewhere He has designated some of it as clear and some as ambiguous. One must therefore distinguish the perfection and consistency that apply to the whole Quran from the clarity and ambiguity that apply to particular parts of it. He says:

Allah, Most High:

“Alif, Lām, Rā. A Book whose verses have been perfected and then explained in detail.”

He thus states that He has perfected all its verses. He also says:

“Allah has sent down the best discourse: a Book, mutually consistent, with recurring passages.”

He thus states that the whole of it is mutually consistent. Judgment means distinguishing between two things; hence a judge settles the dispute between two litigants. Judgment distinguishes between things that resemble one another, in both knowledge and action, by discerning truth from falsehood, truthfulness from lying, and benefit from harm. This entails doing what is beneficial and refraining from what is harmful.

Thus, the expressions hakamtu al-safīha and ahkamtuhu mean “I restrained the foolish person,” when one prevents him from acting. Likewise, hakamtu al-dābbata and ahkamtuhā mean “I fitted the animal with a bridle restraint,” when one equips it with a hakama—the part of the bridle that surrounds its jaw. Perfecting something means making it sound and precise. Perfecting speech therefore means distinguishing truth from falsehood in its statements, and right guidance from error in its commands.

The entire Quran is perfectly formed in the sense of being flawlessly composed. Allah has called it “wise,” saying:

“Alif, Lām, Rā. These are the verses of the wise Book.”

Here, hakīm (“wise”) means hākim (“one that judges”). Likewise, He describes it as recounting, saying:

“Indeed, this Quran recounts to the Children of Israel most of that over which they differ.”

He also describes it as giving a ruling, saying:

“Say, ‘Allah gives you a ruling concerning them, as does what is recited to you in the Book.’”

That is, what is recited to you gives you a ruling concerning them. He also describes it as guiding and bringing glad tidings, saying:

“Indeed, this Quran guides to what is most upright and gives glad tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds.”

“Indeed, your speech is conflicting.”

“Turned away from it is whoever is turned away.”

Mutual consistency here means that the discourse is harmonious and coherent, with its various parts confirming one another. If He commands something, He does not command its opposite elsewhere; rather, He commands that same thing, something comparable to it, or something that entails it. If He forbids something, He does not command it elsewhere; rather, He forbids that same thing, something comparable to it, or something that entails it—provided there has been no abrogation.

Likewise, if He affirms something, He does not state its opposite; rather, He affirms it or affirms something that entails it. If He denies something, He does not affirm it; rather, He denies it or denies its necessary consequences. This contrasts with inconsistent discourse, whose parts contradict one another: it affirms something on one occasion and denies it on another, or commands and forbids it at the same time. It also treats equivalent things differently, praising one and condemning the other.

Thus, inconsistent statements here are those that contradict one another, whereas mutually consistent statements are those that agree. This consistency concerns meanings, even when the wording differs. When the meanings agree with, reinforce, harmonize with, bear witness to, and entail one another, the discourse is mutually consistent. This contrasts with contradictory discourse, whose parts oppose one another.

Mutual consistency in this general sense does not conflict with perfection of composition in its general sense; rather, it confirms it. For speech

that is sound and finely composed has parts that confirm rather than contradict one another. This differs from clear differentiation in the specific sense, which is the opposite of resemblance in the specific sense. Resemblance in the specific sense occurs when something resembles another thing in one respect but differs from it in another, so that some people mistakenly think it is that very thing, or is equivalent to it, when it is not. Clear differentiation means distinguishing the two so that neither is confused with the other.

Such resemblance arises only through a feature shared by the two things, while a distinction between them remains. Some people fail to recognize that distinction and thus find the matter confusing, whereas others recognize it. Resemblance that prevents a person from distinguishing between things may therefore be relative to the observer: it confuses some people but not others. Scholars possess knowledge of such matters that dispels this confusion for them. For example, some people confuse what they have been promised in the Hereafter with what they witness in this world, imagining that they are alike. Scholars, however, know that they are not alike, even though they resemble one another in certain respects.

The misleading ambiguities through which some people go astray belong to this category: truth and falsehood resemble one another within them, leaving some people confused. Those who have been granted knowledge of how to distinguish between the two do not confuse truth with falsehood.

Faulty analogy belongs to this category of misleading ambiguities, for it likens one thing, in certain respects, to something that does not resemble it in those respects. Whoever knows how to distinguish between the two things recognizes the difference that dispels the confusion

translated_text:
and the faulty analogy.

Any two things share something in common and differ in something else: they resemble one another in one respect and differ in another. Thus, the ways in which human beings go astray through resemblance and faulty analogy are beyond enumeration. As Imam Ahmad said:

“Most human error arises from interpretation and analogy.”

Interpretation concerns revealed evidence, while analogy concerns rational evidence. It is indeed as he said. Erroneous interpretation occurs only where expressions resemble one another, and erroneous analogy occurs only where meanings resemble one another. Human beings have fallen into most of the kinds of error encompassed by this statement. Matters have gone so far that some who claim true understanding, affirmation of Allah’s oneness, and spiritual knowledge have confused the Lord’s existence with the existence of every existing thing, imagining them to be identical. They have thus made the existence of created things identical to the existence of the Creator. Yet nothing could be further from resembling another thing, being identical to it, being united with it, or indwelling it than the Creator in relation to creation. Those who confuse the Creator’s existence with the existence of all created things, imagining their existence to be His existence, are therefore the most profoundly misguided through such confusion.

This is because existing things share the meaning denoted by the term “existence.” They therefore regarded existence as one, without distinguishing between being one and the same individual entity and being one in kind. They therefore said: “The term ‘existence’ is used homonymously.” Thus they contradicted the agreement of rational people of every persuasion that existence is divided into eternal and originated existence, and other such categories of existing things.

Another group supposed that, if existing things share the meaning denoted by “existence,” there must be something existing outside the mind that they all share. They claimed that unqualified universals exist outside the mind—existence in the abstract, animal in the abstract, body in the abstract, and the like. They thereby contradicted sensory perception, reason, and revelation, and treated what exists in the mind as existing in concrete reality. All of this is a form of confusion arising from resemblance.

Those whom Allah guides distinguish between things even when they share certain aspects, and recognize what unites and distinguishes them, and how they resemble and differ from one another. Such people are not led astray by ambiguous speech, because they consider it together with clear, decisive speech that establishes the distinctions and explains the differences.

For example, the expressions “Indeed, We” and “We,” and other plural forms, may be used by a single person who has partners in an action. They may also be used by a single person of great stature who possesses attributes, each of which stands in the place of an individual, and who has helpers subordinate to him, not partners.

Thus, if a Christian appeals to the words of the Most High:

“Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder,”

and similar passages as evidence for a plurality of gods, then clear, decisive passages, such as His words:

“And your God is one God,”

and other statements admitting only one meaning, dispel whatever

translated_text:
ambiguity there may be. The plural form He uses thus makes clear the greatness, names and attributes that are His due, and the obedience owed to Him by His creatures, angels and others. As for the actual realities to which this points—the realities of His names and attributes, and the hosts He employs in His acts—none but He knows them:

“And none knows the hosts of your Lord except Him.”

This belongs to the ultimate reality of the ambiguous passages, which Allah alone knows. It is otherwise with a human king: when he says, “We have ordered that you be given a grant,” it is understood that he and his assistants—such as his secretary, chamberlain, servant and others—have been instructed accordingly. One may also know the beliefs, intentions and the like from which that action proceeded.

Allah—glorified and exalted is He—does not disclose to His servants the actual realities of His attributes and the characteristics of the Last Day about which He has informed them. Nor do they know the actual realities of the wisdom He intends through His creation and command, or of the will and power from which these proceed.

This makes clear that ambiguity occurs in univocal terms just as it occurs in homonymous terms that are not univocal, even when the ambiguity is removed by a qualification or identification that distinguishes one of the two kinds. For example, when it is said:

“Therein are rivers of water,”

the water is specifically associated with Paradise, so the distinction between it and the water of this world becomes clear. Yet the actual reality of what distinguishes that water remains unknown to us. Together with what Allah has prepared for His righteous servants—what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived—it belongs to the ultimate reality that Allah alone knows.

and likewise what His names and attributes uniquely denote—a reality known only to Him.

For this reason, the imams, including Imam Ahmad and others, censured the Jahmiyyah and those like them—who distort words from their proper places—for interpreting passages of the Quran that they found ambiguous in ways other than their correct interpretation. Ahmad said this in the book he wrote to refute the heretics and the Jahmiyyah concerning the ambiguous passages of the Quran about which they harboured doubts and which they interpreted incorrectly.

He censured them precisely because they interpreted these passages incorrectly. In that work, he discussed passages whose meanings were unclear to them, even though they were not unclear to others, and censured them for interpreting those passages incorrectly. He did not reject the term ta’wīl altogether. As explained earlier, ta’wīl may mean an explanation that clarifies what Allah intends; this is not blameworthy but praiseworthy. It may also mean the actual reality whose knowledge Allah has reserved to Himself; that is known only to Him. We have discussed this at length elsewhere.

Those who fail to understand this become inconsistent in their statements. For example, some say that ta’wīl is invalid and that the wording must be understood according to its apparent meaning. They cite the words of the Most High:

“And no one knows its interpretation except Allah.”

They invoke this verse to invalidate ta’wīl, but this is a contradiction on their part: the verse establishes that there is a ta’wīl known only to Allah, whereas they reject ta’wīl altogether. Their error lies in failing to recognise that the ta’wīl whose knowledge Allah has reserved to Himself is the actual reality known only to Him.

translated_text:
As for blameworthy and invalid ta’wīl, it is the interpretation offered by those who distort the texts and introduce religious innovations. They interpret them incorrectly and claim to divert the wording from what it signifies to something else, without evidence requiring this. They claim that its apparent meaning entails an objectionable consequence comparable to what necessarily follows from what they themselves affirm through reason. They then redirect it to meanings comparable to those they have denied it conveys. Thus, what they deny is of the same kind as what they affirm. If what they affirm is true and possible, then so is what they deny; and if what they deny is false and impossible, then so is what they affirm.

Those who reject ta’wīl altogether and cite the words of the Most High:

“And no one knows its interpretation except Allah.”

may suppose that we have been addressed in the Quran with words that no one understands, that have no meaning, or from which nothing can be understood. Besides being false, this is self-contradictory. If we understand nothing from it, we cannot say that it has an interpretation that either contradicts or accords with its apparent meaning; for it may have a valid meaning. That valid meaning does not contradict any apparent meaning known to us, since, according to their claim, it has no apparent meaning. Its signification of that meaning would therefore not contradict an apparent meaning, and so would not constitute ta’wīl.

Nor, on this assumption, may we deny that it signifies meanings unknown to us, for we may not know the meanings it signifies. Moreover, if we do not understand the wording and what it signifies, we are even less likely to know the meanings it does not signify. This is because wording indicates what is intended by it more strongly than it indicates what is not intended by it. Thus, if the wording gives no indication of a meaning

 إنَّهُ مُشَبِّهٌ وَمُنَازِعُهُمْ يَقُولُ: ذَلِكَ الْمَعْنَى لَيْسَ مِنْ التَّشْبِيهِ.
translated_text:
The Sixth Principle

Someone may say:

In this matter, there must be a criterion by which to distinguish what is possible with respect to Allah from what is impossible, both in negation and in affirmation. Merely denying likeness, or affirming without qualification while denying likeness, is not a sound basis. For any two things have something in common and something that distinguishes them.

If someone denies an attribute on the grounds that affirming it entails likeness, he should be told: “If you mean that one is identical to the other in every respect, this is false. But if you mean that one resembles the other in some respects but not others, or shares the same name, then this also applies to everything else you affirm. You have only established evidence against likeness and equivalence as you yourselves have defined them: whatever is possible for one is possible for the other, whatever is impossible for one is impossible for the other, and whatever is necessary for one is necessary for the other. Clearly, no rational person who understands what he is saying would affirm likeness in this sense, for its impossibility is self-evident to reason. Denying this, however, does not entail denying resemblance in certain respects, as with names and attributes used in a shared sense.”

Yet some people define likeness in a particular sense, then say of anyone who affirms that meaning: “He likens Allah to His creation.” Their opponent, however, says: “That meaning does not constitute likeness.”

translated_text:
A distinction may also be drawn between the terms “likening” and “asserting equivalence.” The Muʿtazilah and others who deny the divine attributes say:

“Anyone who affirms a beginningless attribute for Allah likens Him to another and asserts equivalence between them.”

Thus, anyone who says that Allah has beginningless knowledge or beginningless power is, in their view, guilty of such likening and equivalence. This is because most of them regard beginninglessness as the most distinctive characteristic of God. Whoever affirms a beginningless attribute for Him has therefore, in their view, affirmed a beginningless counterpart to Allah, and on this basis they describe him as someone who asserts equivalence.

Those who affirm the divine attributes do not agree with them. Rather, they say: “His most distinctive characteristics are those that belong to no one else, such as His being the Lord of all worlds, His knowing all things, His having power over all things, His being the One God, and the like.” An attribute cannot itself be described by any of these characteristics.

Among those who affirm the attributes, some do not say that the attributes are beginningless. Instead, they say: “The Lord, with His attributes, is beginningless.” Others say: “He is beginningless, and His attribute is beginningless,” but do not say: “He and His attributes are both beginningless.”

Still others say: “He and His attributes are both beginningless.” However, they say: “This does not entail that an attribute shares any of His distinctive characteristics. Beginninglessness is not a distinctive characteristic of the essence stripped of attributes, but of the essence possessing attributes. Indeed, in their view, an essence stripped of attributes does not exist at all, let alone possess beginninglessness as its distinctive characteristic.”

They may also say: “The essence is characterized by beginninglessness, and the attributes are characterized by beginninglessness; yet the attributes are neither a god nor a lord, just as the Prophet came into existence and his attributes came into existence, yet his attributes are not a prophet.”

translated_text:
Thus, when these people describe those who affirm the divine attributes as guilty of “likening” and “asserting equivalence,” they do so on the basis of beliefs that the latter dispute. Those who affirm the attributes then reply:

“Granted that some people may call this meaning ‘likening’ in their terminology, neither reason nor revelation has ruled it out. What must be denied is only what scriptural and rational proofs negate. The Quran has denied that Allah has any likeness, equal, rival, or the like.”

However, those who affirm the attributes say that, in Arabic usage, an attribute is neither the likeness, equal, nor rival of the one it describes, and therefore does not fall within the scope of the scriptural text. As for reason, it has not ruled out what the Muʿtazilah call “likening” in their terminology.

They also say:

“Attributes can subsist only in a spatially situated body, and all bodies are alike. If attributes subsisted in Him, it would necessarily follow that He was like all other bodies. This is what constitutes likening.”

This is also asserted by many of those who affirm the divine attributes but deny His being above the Throne, deny that acts of His choosing subsist in Him, and deny other such matters. They say:

“Attributes may subsist in what is not a body. Being above the world, however, is possible only if He is a body. If we affirmed His being above it, this would necessarily entail that He is a body; and since all bodies are alike, likening would necessarily follow.”

For this reason, you find that they describe anyone who affirms His being above the world and similar matters as one who likens Him to others, but do not describe anyone who affirms His hearing, sight, speech, and similar attributes in this way. This is the position expressed by the author of al-Irshād and others like him.
