translated_text:
Likewise, al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā and others who affirm the divine attributes and His being above the world agree with them that all bodies are alike. However, they treat His being above the world as an attribute known through revelation, as in the earlier of al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā’s two positions. Discussion of it thus follows the same approach as discussion of His Face. They may also say that what they affirm is not incompatible with corporeality, just as they say concerning the other attributes. Anyone who reflects rationally will find that what they deny stands on the same footing as what they affirm: there is no difference.

The arguments of all these groups rest on the premises that affirming the attributes necessarily entails ascribing corporeality to Allah, and that all bodies are alike. Those who affirm the attributes respond sometimes by rejecting the first premise, sometimes by rejecting the second, sometimes by rejecting both, and sometimes by asking for clarification of what is meant.

There is no doubt that their assertion that all bodies are alike is false, whether they define a body as something that can be pointed to, something that subsists in itself, something that exists, something composed of matter and form, or something similar. If, however, they define it as something composed of indivisible atoms and assume that these atoms are all alike, their conclusion depends on the validity of that account, on establishing the existence of indivisible atoms, and on establishing that they are all alike. Most rational thinkers disagree with them on these matters.

translated_text:
those who are loyal to Abū Bakr and ‘Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, on the premise that whoever loves them hates ‘Alī, may Allah be pleased with him, and that whoever hates him is a Nāsibī (one hostile to ‘Alī). Ahl al-Sunnah dispute the first premise.

For this reason, these people say that two things do not resemble one another in one respect while differing in another. Most rational thinkers disagree. We have discussed this at length elsewhere, setting out the arguments of those who maintain that all bodies are alike and those who deny this, and demonstrating the falsity of the former position.

Furthermore, relying on this approach to deny likeness is invalid. For if it is established that all bodies are alike, they deny such likeness only through the argument by which they deny that He is a body. If it is established that this entails corporeality, and that corporeality is impossible for Him, this alone suffices to deny it; there is no need to deny what is termed “likening.” However, the denial of corporeality is based on denying this likeness, by saying: “If such-and-such were affirmed of Him, He would be a body.” Then it is said: “All bodies are alike, so they must share what is necessary, possible, and impossible for them; yet this is impossible for Him.”

But in that case, whoever follows this approach relies on denying corporeality in order to deny likeness. Thus, the foundation of his denial is the denial that He is a body. This is another approach, which we shall discuss, if Allah wills.

 إنَّ الشَّيْءَ إذَا شَابَهَ غَيْرَهُ مِنْ وَجْهٍ جَازَ عَلَيْهِ مَا يَجُوزُ عَلَيْهِ مِنْ ذَلِكَ الْوَجْهِ وَوَجَبَ لَهُ مَا وَجَبَ لَهُ وَامْتَنَعَ عَلَيْهِ مَا امْتَنَعَ عَلَيْهِ.
قِيلَ:
 هَبْ أَنَّ الْأَمْرَ كَذَلِكَ وَلَكِنْ إذَا كَانَ ذَلِكَ الْقَدْرُ الْمُشْتَرَكُ لَا يَسْتَلْزِمُ إثْبَاتَ مَا يَمْتَنِعُ عَلَى الرَّبِّ سُبْحَانَهُ وَلَا نَفْيُ مَا يَسْتَحِقُّهُ لَمْ يَكُنْ مُمْتَنِعًا كَمَا إذَا قِيلَ: إنَّهُ مَوْجُودٌ حَيٌّ عَلِيمٌ سَمِيعٌ بَصِيرٌ وَقَدْ سُمِّيَ بَعْضُ الْمَخْلُوقَاتِ حَيًّا سَمْعِيًّا عَلِيمًا بَصِيرًا فَإِذَا قِيلَ: يَلْزَمُ أَنَّهُ يَجُوزُ عَلَيْهِ مَا يَجُوزُ عَلَى ذَلِكَ مِنْ جِهَةِ كَوْنِهِ مَوْجُودًا حَيًّا عَلِيمًا سَمِيعًا بَصِيرًا قِيلَ: لَازِمُ هَذَا الْقَدْرِ الْمُشْتَرَكِ لَيْسَ مُمْتَنِعًا عَلَى الرَّبِّ تَعَالَى فَإِنَّ ذَلِكَ لَا يَقْتَضِي حُدُوثًا وَلَا إمْكَانًا وَلَا نَقْصًا وَلَا شَيْئًا مِمَّا يُنَافِي صِفَاتِ الرُّبُوبِيَّةِ
translated_text:
The point here, however, is simply this: relying solely on the denial of likeness to deny whatever one seeks to deny serves no purpose, since any two things resemble one another in some respect and differ in another. This is unlike relying on the denial of deficiency, defect, and similar imperfections from which He—glorified be He—is free, for this is a sound approach. Likewise, affirming His attributes of perfection while denying that anyone else is His equal in them denies equality in what rightfully belongs to Him. This is the essence of monotheism: nothing shares with Him anything that is exclusively His. He possesses every attribute of perfection in a manner in which no one is His equal. Hence, the position of the early generations of the Muslim community and its leading scholars was to affirm the attributes with which He described Himself and to deny that He is like any created being.

If it is said:
“When one thing resembles another in some respect, whatever is possible for the latter in that respect is possible for the former; whatever is necessary for the latter is necessary for the former, and whatever is impossible for the latter is impossible for the former.”

The reply is:
“Granted that this is so. But if that shared aspect entails neither affirming what is impossible for the Lord—glorified be He—nor denying what rightfully belongs to Him, then it is not impossible. For example, it is said that He exists and is living, knowing, hearing, and seeing; some created beings have also been described as living, sam‘ī (pertaining to hearing), knowing, and seeing. If it is then said, ‘It follows that whatever is possible for such a created being insofar as it exists and is living, knowing, hearing, and seeing must also be possible for Him,’ the reply is: ‘What this shared aspect entails is not impossible for the Lord Most High, for it entails neither coming into existence, nor contingency, nor deficiency, nor anything incompatible with the attributes of lordship.’”

وَالْمَعَانِي الَّتِي يُوصَفُ بِهَا الرَّبُّ تَعَالَى كَالْحَيَاةِ وَالْعِلْمِ وَالْقُدْرَةِ بَلْ الْوُجُودُ وَالثُّبُوتُ وَالْحَقِيقَةُ وَنَحْوُ ذَلِكَ:
 تَجِبُ لَوَازِمُهَا فَإِنَّ ثُبُوتَ الْمَلْزُومِ يَقْتَضِي ثُبُوتَ اللَّازِمِ، وَخَصَائِصُ الْمَخْلُوقِ الَّتِي يَجِبُ تَنْزِيهُ الرَّبِّ عَنْهَا لَيْسَتْ مِنْ لَوَازِمِ ذَلِكَ أَصْلًا بَلْ تِلْكَ مِنْ لَوَازِمِ مَا يَخْتَصُّ بِالْمَخْلُوقِ مِنْ وُجُودٍ وَحَيَاةٍ وَعِلْمٍ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ
translated_text:
For the shared aspect is what is denoted by “existence,” “an existent being,” “life,” “living,” “knowledge,” “knowing,” “hearing,” “sight,” “one who hears,” “one who sees,” “power,” or “powerful.” This shared aspect is an unrestricted universal, not exclusive to either of the two. Thus, they share neither what is exclusive to the contingent being that has come into existence nor what is exclusive to the necessarily existent, eternal Being. Whatever is exclusive to either cannot be shared by both.

If the aspect they share is an attribute of perfection, such as existence, life, knowledge, or power, and contains nothing indicating the distinctive characteristics of created beings—just as it indicates none of the distinctive characteristics of the Creator—then there is nothing objectionable whatsoever in affirming it. Indeed, affirming this is a necessary consequence of existence: any two existent beings must share something of this kind. Whoever denies this must consequently deny the existence of every existent being. Hence, when the leading scholars recognized that this was the true implication of the Jahmiyyah’s position, they called them “negators.” Jahm denied that Allah could be called a “thing,” though the Jahmiyyah sometimes said, “He is a thing unlike other things.” Thus, denying any shared aspect whatsoever entails universal negation.

The meanings conveyed by descriptions of the Lord Most High—such as life, knowledge, and power, and indeed existence, actuality, reality, and the like—have implications that must necessarily hold. For whenever something holds, its necessary implications also hold. The distinctive characteristics of created beings, from which the Lord must be declared free, are not among the necessary implications of these meanings at all. Rather, they are necessary implications of the existence, life, knowledge, and similar qualities peculiar to created beings.

translated_text:
And Allah, glorified be He, is free of the distinctive characteristics of created beings and of anything that necessarily entails those characteristics. Whoever understands this point well and reflects upon it will find most doubts dispelled and recognize the errors of many intelligent people in this matter.

This has been discussed at length in many places, where it has been explained that the universal shared aspect exists in external reality only in a particular, qualified form. For existent beings to share something means that they resemble one another in that respect, and that the same general meaning applies to each. In external reality, however, neither shares with the other anything actually existing within it; rather, every existent being is distinct from others in its essence, attributes, and actions.

Such being the case, many people are inconsistent in this matter. At times, a person supposes that affirming the shared aspect necessarily entails the false assimilation of Allah to created beings. He therefore uses this as an argument for denying those attributes he thinks should be denied, seeking to avoid anything that would entail such assimilation. At other times, he realizes that this shared aspect must be affirmed under a given assumption, and uses that recognition to defend the attributes he does affirm against those negators who invoke the same argument.

The considerable confusion surrounding this matter has given rise to doubts over whether the Lord’s existence is identical with His essence or additional to it, and whether the word “existence” is predicated equivocally, univocally, or with gradation in its meaning. and over whether the nonexistent is a thing, and whether the existence of existing things is additional to their essences. Leading speculative thinkers have displayed much inconsistency and contradiction on these questions. At times, one of them adopts two mutually contradictory positions and attributes to others views they never expressed; at other times, he remains in doubt and bewilderment.

We have discussed these questions at length, along with the confusion, error, and bewilderment they have occasioned among leading theologians and philosophers, in greater detail than these brief statements can accommodate. We have explained that the correct position is that the existence of each thing in external reality is its essence as it exists in external reality. This differs from its essence as conceived in the mind, which is distinct from what exists externally.

We have also explained that the terms “self,” “thing,” “essence,” “reality,” and the like are all univocal. If they are said to be graded because their meanings admit of differing degrees, then graded predication is a type of univocal predication in its broader sense: what matters is that the term signifies a shared meaning, whether that meaning varies in degree across its instances or is equal in them.

We have explained that the nonexistent is also a thing in knowledge and in the mind, but not in external reality. Thus, there is no distinction between subsistence and existence; rather, the distinction is between existence in knowledge and existence in external reality. Nevertheless, what is present in knowledge is not the existent reality itself, but the knowledge that belongs to the knower and inheres in him. translated_text:
Section

Even more unsound is the approach taken by those who deny the attributes, or some of them, when they seek to declare Him free of things from which He must indeed be declared free, and whose attribution to Him constitutes some of the gravest forms of disbelief. For example, they seek to declare Him free of sorrow, weeping, and the like, and to refute those Jews who say that He wept over the Flood until His eyes became inflamed and the angels visited Him in His illness, as well as those who ascribe divinity to a human being and claim that he is Allah.

Many people argue against these claims by denying corporeality, spatial location, and the like. They say: “If He possessed these deficiencies and afflictions, He would be a body or have spatial location, and that is impossible.” By adopting such an approach, they have allowed these heretics who deny the names and attributes to gain the upper hand over them. This method does not achieve its intended purpose, for several reasons.

First:

Attributing these deficiencies and afflictions to Allah Most High is more evidently invalid, both rationally and religiously, than denying spatial location and corporeality. The latter involves ambiguity, dispute, and obscurity that are absent from the former. That someone who attributes such deficiencies to Him has committed disbelief is necessarily known in the religion of Islam.

A proof serves to make known and clarify what it establishes. It is therefore inadmissible to establish what is more evident and clearer by means of what is less evident, just as this is not done when formulating definitions.

original_text:
الْوَجْهُ الثَّانِي:

 قَالَتْ لَهُمْ الْمُثْبِتَةُ:
 وَأَنْتُمْ قَدْ قُلْتُمْ: إنَّهُ حَيٌّ عَلِيمٌ قَدِيرٌ.
 وَقُلْتُمْ:
 لَيْسَ بِجِسْمِ؛
 وَأَنْتُمْ لَا تَعْلَمُونَ مَوْجُودًا حَيًّا عَالِمًا قَادِرًا إلَّا جِسْمًا فَقَدْ أَثْبَتُّمُوهُ عَلَى خِلَافِ مَا عَلِمْتُمْ فَكَذَلِكَ نَحْنُ وَقَالُوا لَهُمْ:
 أَنْتُمْ أَثْبَتُّمْ حَيًّا عَالِمًا قَادِرًا؛ بِلَا حَيَاةٍ وَلَا عِلْمٍ وَلَا قُدْرَةٍ وَهَذَا تَنَاقُضٌ يُعْلَمُ بِضَرُورَةِ الْعَقْلِ
translated_text:
Second:

Those who ascribe these attributes to Him could say, “We do not affirm corporeality or spatial location,” just as those who affirm the attributes while denying corporeality say. Their dispute would thus become like the dispute involving those who affirm speech and the attributes of perfection. The arguments of those who ascribe attributes of perfection to Allah and those who ascribe attributes of deficiency to Him would then be the same, and those who deny the attributes would refute both groups by the same method. This is utterly unsound.

Third:

These people deny the attributes of perfection by this same method, whereas His possessing the attributes of perfection is necessary and established by both reason and revelation. This therefore demonstrates the unsoundness of this method.

Fourth:

Those who follow this method contradict themselves. Whenever one of them affirms something, another holds him to the implications of what they both affirm; likewise, whenever one of them denies something, another holds him to the implications of what they both deny.

Thus, when those who deny the attributes, such as the Muʿtazila, say to those who affirm attributes—such as life, knowledge, power, speech, hearing, and sight—“This is corporealism, because these attributes are accidents, and an accident can subsist only in a body; or because we know of nothing possessing attributes except a body,” those who affirm the attributes reply:

“Yet you yourselves have said that He is living, knowing, and powerful, and that He is not a body. You know of no existing being that is living, knowing, and powerful except a body. You have thus affirmed Him in a manner unlike what you have known; we do likewise.”

They also say to them:

“You have affirmed one who is living, knowing, and powerful, yet without life, knowledge, or power. This is a contradiction that reason necessarily recognizes.”

 لَمْ يَسْلُكْهُ أَحَدٌ مِنْ السَّلَفِ وَالْأَئِمَّةِ فَلَمْ يَنْطِقْ أَحَدٌ مِنْهُمْ فِي حَقِّ اللَّهِ بِالْجِسْمِ لَا نَفْيًا وَلَا إثْبَاتًا وَلَا بِالْجَوْهَرِ وَالتَّحَيُّزِ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ لِأَنَّهَا عِبَارَاتٌ مُجْمَلَةٌ لَا تُحِقُّ حَقًّا وَلَا تُبْطِلُ بَاطِلًا وَلِهَذَا لَمْ يَذْكُرْ اللَّهُ فِي كِتَابِهِ فِيمَا أَنْكَرَهُ عَلَى الْيَهُودِ وَغَيْرِهِمْ مِنْ الْكُفَّارِ: مَا هُوَ مِنْ هَذَا النَّوْعِ؛ بَلْ هَذَا هُوَ مِنْ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبْتَدَعِ الَّذِي أَنْكَرَهُ السَّلَفُ وَالْأَئِمَّةُ.
translated_text:
Then, when these affirmers say to those who affirm that He is pleased, becomes angry, loves, and hates—or who describe Him as rising above, descending, coming, and arriving, or as having a face, a hand, and the like—“This entails corporealism, because we know of nothing described in this way except a body,” those who affirm these attributes reply:

“Yet you yourselves have described Him as possessing life, knowledge, power, hearing, sight, and speech, and the same reasoning applies to these. If only a body can be described by these attributes, the same holds for the others. If something that is not a body can be described by one set of attributes, the same holds for the other. To distinguish between them is therefore to distinguish between equivalent cases.”

Thus, since this method of refuting those who ascribe deficiencies to Allah Most High is unsound, none of the early generations or imams adopted it. None of them spoke of Allah in terms of a body, whether to deny or affirm it, nor in terms of substance, spatial location, or the like. These are ambiguous expressions that neither establish any truth nor refute any falsehood. Accordingly, nothing of this kind appears among the things Allah condemned in the Jews and other disbelievers in His Book. Rather, this belongs to the innovated discourse that the early generations and imams condemned.

 يَأْكُلُ لَا كَأَكْلِ الْعِبَادِ وَيَشْرَبُ لَا كَشُرْبِهِمْ وَيَبْكِي وَيَحْزَنُ لَا كَبُكَائِهِمْ وَلَا حُزْنِهِمْ؛ كَمَا يُقَالُ يَضْحَكُ لَا كَضَحِكِهِمْ وَيَفْرَحُ لَا كَفَرَحِهِمْ وَيَتَكَلَّمُ لَا كَكَلَامِهِمْ.
 وَلَجَازَ أَنْ يُقَالَ:
 لَهُ أَعْضَاءٌ كَثِيرَةٌ لَا كَأَعْضَائِهِمْ كَمَا قِيلَ: لَهُ وَجْهٌ لَا كَوُجُوهِهِمْ وَيَدَانِ لَا كَأَيْدِيهِمْ. حَتَّى يَذْكُرَ الْمَعِدَةَ وَالْأَمْعَاءَ وَالذَّكَرَ وَغَيْرَ ذَلِكَ مِمَّا يَتَعَالَى اللَّهُ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ عَنْهُ سُبْحَانَهُ وَتَعَالَى عَمَّا يَقُولُ الظَّالِمُونَ عُلُوًّا كَبِيرًا.
 فَإِنَّهُ يُقَالُ لِمَنْ نَفَى ذَلِكَ مَعَ إثْبَاتِ الصِّفَاتِ الْخَبَرِيَّةِ وَغَيْرِهَا مِنْ الصِّفَاتِ:
 مَا الْفَرْقُ بَيْنَ هَذَا وَمَا أَثْبَتَّهُ إذَا نَفَيْت التَّشْبِيهَ وَجَعَلْت مُجَرَّدَ نَفْيِ التَّشْبِيهِ كَافِيًا فِي الْإِثْبَاتِ فَلَا بُدُّ مِنْ إثْبَاتِ فَرْقٍ فِي نَفْسِ الْأَمْرِ
translated_text:
Section

As for methods of affirmation, it is likewise clear that merely denying resemblance is not enough to establish what is being affirmed. If it were enough, it would be permissible to ascribe to Him—glory be to Him—almost innumerable bodily parts and actions that are impossible for Him, while denying resemblance. It would also be permissible to ascribe to Him deficiencies that cannot be attributed to Him, while denying resemblance—as when someone fabricates claims about Him by ascribing to Him weeping, sorrow, hunger, and thirst while denying resemblance.

Such a fabricator might say:

“He eats, but not as His servants eat; He drinks, but not as they drink; He weeps and grieves, but not as they weep and grieve—just as it is said, ‘He laughs, but not as they laugh; He rejoices, but not as they rejoice; and He speaks, but not as they speak.’”

It would likewise be permissible to say:

“He has many bodily parts, but not like theirs—just as it is said, ‘He has a face, but not like their faces, and two hands, but not like their hands.’”

This could extend even to mentioning a stomach, intestines, a male organ, and other things far beneath the majesty of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Glory be to Him! Exalted is He far above what the wrongdoers say.

For someone who denies these things while affirming the attributes known through revelation and other attributes would be asked:

“What is the difference between these things and what you have affirmed, if you deny resemblance and consider that denial alone sufficient for affirmation?”

There must, therefore, be a distinction between them in reality.

 كُلَّمَا نُفِيَ صِفَاتُ الْكَمَالِ الثَّابِتَةِ لِلَّهِ فَهُوَ مُنَزَّهٌ عَنْهُ فَإِنَّ ثُبُوتَ أَحَدِ
translated_text:
If, then, he says:

“The basis for this distinction is revelation: whatever revelation conveys is affirmed, whereas whatever it does not convey is not affirmed,”

he is told, first: Revelation is the truthful messenger’s report of things as they actually are. Whatever the truthful messenger reports, whether by way of negation or affirmation, is true. A report is evidence for what it reports, but evidence does not entail the converse: its absence does not necessarily entail the absence of what it indicates. Thus, something not mentioned in revelation may nevertheless be established in reality, provided revelation has not denied it.

It is known that revelation has not denied these things by their particular names. One must therefore identify what in revelation rules them out; otherwise, it would not then be permissible to deny them, just as it would not be permissible to affirm them.

Furthermore, there must be a distinction in reality between what is affirmed of Him and what is denied of Him. Things alike with respect to possibility, necessity, and impossibility cannot be assigned different statuses in these respects. What is denied must therefore differ from what is affirmed in some respect that warrants its denial; likewise, what is affirmed must differ from what is denied in some respect that warrants its affirmation.

This may also be expressed as follows: There must be a reason requiring the denial of whatever must be denied of Allah, just as there must be a reason establishing whatever is affirmed of Him. If revelation is sufficient, then it reports things as they actually are. What, then, is the distinction in reality between the two?

The reply is:

Whatever negates the attributes of perfection established for Allah is something He is exalted above, for the affirmation of one of

translated_text:
two opposites entails the negation of the other. Thus, when it is known that He exists necessarily in Himself and is necessarily without beginning, it is known that nonexistence and coming into being are impossible for Him. It is also known that He is independent of everything other than Himself. For whatever depends on something else for any of its own needs does not exist by itself alone, but by itself together with that other which supplies what it needs; it therefore cannot exist without it.

He—glorified is He—is independent of everything other than Himself, and so He is exalted above whatever contradicts His independence. He—glorified is He—is powerful and strong, and so He is exalted above whatever contradicts His power and strength. He—glorified is He—is the Ever-Living, Self-Subsisting Sustainer of all, and so He is exalted above whatever contradicts His life, His self-subsistence, or His sustaining of all things.

In short, revelation has affirmed for Him the most beautiful names and attributes of perfection that have been transmitted. Revelation therefore denies whatever contradicts them, just as it denies that He has any likeness or equal. For affirming something negates its opposite and whatever entails that opposite. Reason recognizes this negation just as it recognizes the affirmation of the opposite: affirming either of two opposites negates the other and whatever entails it.

Thus, the ways of knowing that whatever the Lord is exalted above must be denied of Him are extensive. There is no need to confine them merely to denying resemblance and corporeality, as those deficient in understanding and negligent in their efforts have done. They have contradicted themselves in this regard and distinguished between things that are alike, to the point that whenever anyone affirms something, whoever denies it argues against him that it entails resemblance. Likewise, the Qarmatians argued for denying all things, until they even denied negation itself, saying:

translated_text:
“One must not say that He exists or that He does not exist, nor that He is living or that He is not living, for that would liken Him to what exists or to what does not exist.” This entails denying both sides of a contradiction—something whose impossibility is utterly plain. Moreover, these people necessarily liken Him to nonexistent things, impossibilities, and inanimate objects to a far greater degree than the resemblance to perfect living beings from which they sought to flee. The ways of declaring Him exalted and holy above all that He is free from are extensive; there is no need for this approach.

It has already been explained that whatever is denied of Him—glorified is He—is denied in a manner that entails affirmation, since mere negation contains neither praise nor perfection. Nonexistent things can be described through negation, and what does not exist does not resemble existing things; yet this is no praise of it. Resembling a deficient being in its deficiencies is itself a deficiency in every case, just as being identical to a created being in any attribute constitutes a likeness and resemblance above which the Lord—blessed and exalted is He—is far exalted. Deficiency is the opposite of perfection.

For example, it is known that He is living, and death is the opposite of life, so He is exalted above it. Likewise, sleep and drowsiness are contrary to the perfection of life, for sleep is the brother of death. Fatigue, too, is a deficiency in power and strength. Eating, drinking, and similar things involve dependence upon something other than oneself, just as seeking another’s assistance, relying on another’s support, and similar things entail dependence upon and need for that other. Anyone who needs someone to bear him or help sustain his being and his actions is dependent upon him

One who eats and drinks has a hollow interior, whereas one who is solid, without a hollow interior, is more perfect than one who eats and drinks. This is why the angels have no hollow interiors and neither eat nor drink. It has already been explained that the Creator is more entitled to every perfection established for a created being, and more entitled to be free of every deficiency from which a created being is free. Revelation has denied these things of Him in several places, as in His statement, exalted is He:

“Allah, the Eternal Refuge.”

Al-Samad is He who has no hollow interior and neither eats nor drinks. This surah describes the Most Merciful, or is the foundation of this subject. He also says concerning the Messiah and his mother:

“The Messiah, son of Mary, was not but a messenger; other messengers have passed on before him. And his mother was a woman of truth. They both used to eat food.”

He thus made their eating food evidence that they were not divine. This demonstrates, all the more certainly, that He is exalted above such things. The liver, spleen, and similar organs serve the functions of eating and drinking. The Self-Sufficient One, who is exalted above these functions, is therefore exalted above the organs that serve them. The hand is different, for it serves work and action, and He—glorified is He—is described as working and acting, since these are attributes of perfection. One who can act is more perfect than one who cannot.

He—glorified is He—is exalted above having a consort or offspring, and above the organs and means associated with that. Likewise, weeping and sorrow entail weakness and incapacity, above which He—glorified is He—is exalted. Joy and anger, by contrast, are attributes of perfection. translated_text:
incapacity, knowledge rather than ignorance, life rather than death, hearing rather than deafness, sight rather than blindness, and speech rather than muteness, so too He is described as possessing joy rather than sorrow, laughter rather than weeping, and so forth.

Moreover, reason has established what revelation affirms: that He—glorified is He—has no equal or peer, and nothing is like Him. His reality therefore cannot be like the reality of any created being, nor can the reality of any of His attributes be like that of any attribute of created beings. It is thus known with certainty that He does not belong to any category of created beings: neither angels, nor the heavens, nor stars, nor air, nor water, nor earth, nor human beings, nor their bodies or souls, nor anything else. Indeed, it is known that His reality is further removed from resemblance to anything in existence than all other realities are, and that any resemblance between Him and any of them is more remote than the resemblance between the reality of one created being and that of another. For if two realities are alike, whatever is possible for either is possible for the other, and whatever is necessary for either is necessary for the other.

It would then follow that nonexistence and need, which are possible for a created being brought into existence, would also be possible for the beginningless Creator, whose existence is intrinsically necessary. What is affirmed of the one would also have to be affirmed of the other, including necessary existence and passing away. Thus, the same thing would be both intrinsically necessary and not intrinsically necessary, both existent and nonexistent. This combines two contradictories.

This demonstrates the falsehood of the position of those who liken Allah to His creation, saying, “Sight like my sight,” or “A hand like my hand,” and similar things. Exalted is Allah far above what they say!

translated_text:
The purpose here is not to give an exhaustive account of what is affirmed of Him, what He is declared free of, or the ways of establishing these matters, for this is discussed at length elsewhere. Rather, the purpose here is to draw attention to the general principles governing these matters and the ways of establishing them.

Whatever revelation neither affirms nor denies, and for which reason provides no grounds for either affirmation or negation, we leave unaddressed, neither affirming nor denying it. Thus, we affirm what we know to be established, deny what we know to be negated, and remain silent about what we do not know to be either negated or established. And Allah knows best.

translated_text:
Section

As for the second principle—devoting worship to Allah alone, which encompasses belief in both divine law and divine decree—we say:

It is essential to believe in Allah’s creation and command. We must believe that Allah is the Creator, Lord, and Sovereign of all things; that He has power over all things; that whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass; and that there is no might or power except through Allah. He knew what would happen before it happened, ordained all decrees, and recorded them wherever He willed. As the Most High says:

“Do you not know that Allah knows what is in heaven and earth? Indeed, that is in a Record. Indeed, that is easy for Allah.”

It is reported in the authentic collection that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah ordained the destinies of all creatures fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth, and His Throne was upon the water.”

We must also believe that Allah commanded that He alone be worshipped, without any partner, just as He created the jinn and humankind to worship Him. For this purpose He sent His messengers and revealed His books. Worship of Him entails

utter humility before Him and perfect love for Him. This entails complete obedience to Him:

“Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah.”

The Most High has said:

“We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by Allah’s permission.”

And the Most High has said:

“If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you and forgive you your sins.”

And the Most High has said:

“Ask those of Our messengers whom We sent before you: Did We appoint any gods besides the Most Merciful to be worshipped?”

“We did not send any messenger before you without revealing to him: There is no deity except Me, so worship Me.”

And the Most High has said:

“He has prescribed for you as religion what He enjoined upon Noah, that which We have revealed to you, and what We enjoined upon Abraham, Moses, and Jesus: ‘Establish the religion and do not be divided in it.’ What you call them to is hard for those who associate partners with Allah.”

And the Most High has said:

“O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds. Indeed, I know all that you do.”

“And indeed, this community of yours is one community, and I am your Lord, so fear Me.”

Thus, He commanded the messengers to establish the religion and not to be divided in it. Hence the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in an authentic hadith:

“We prophets share one religion. The prophets are brothers with the same father and different mothers. Indeed, I am the closest of all people to the son of Mary; there is no prophet between him and me.”

This religion is Islam, and Allah accepts no other religion, whether from earlier or later generations, for all the prophets followed the religion of Islam. Allah Most High said concerning Noah:

“Relate to them the account of Noah, when he said to his people: ‘O my people, if you find my presence among you burdensome, along with my reminders

of Allah’s signs—then in Allah I put my trust. So resolve upon your course, together with your partners.’” Up to His saying:

“And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims.”

He said concerning Abraham:

“And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself?”

Up to His saying:

“When his Lord said to him, ‘Submit,’ he said, ‘I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds.’”

Up to His saying:

“So do not die except as Muslims.”

He said concerning Moses:

“O my people, if you have believed in Allah, then put your trust in Him, if you are Muslims.”

He said in the account of the Messiah:

“And when I inspired the disciples, ‘Believe in Me and in My messenger,’ they said, ‘We believe, so bear witness that we are Muslims.’”

He said concerning the earlier prophets:

“The prophets who submitted to Allah judged by it for the Jews.”

He said concerning Balqīs that she said:

“My Lord, I have indeed wronged myself, and I have submitted, together with Solomon, to Allah, the Lord of the worlds.”

Islam entails submission to Allah alone. Whoever submits to Him and to another associates partners with Him, while whoever does not submit to Him is too proud to worship Him. Both the one who associates partners with Him and the one who is too proud to worship Him are disbelievers. Submission to Him alone entails worshipping Him alone and obeying Him alone.

Religion consists in obedience to Him and worship of Him in both acts; only an outward aspect of the act varies, namely, the direction faced in prayer. Likewise, the messengers’ religion is one, even though their laws, prescribed ways, prayer directions, and rites differ. Such differences do not prevent their religion from being one, just as they did not prevent this within the law of a single messenger.

Allah Most High made it part of the messengers’ religion that the first of them should announce the coming of the last and believe in him, and that the last should affirm the truth of the first and believe in him. Allah Most High said:

“And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets: ‘Whatever I give you of Scripture and wisdom, should a messenger then come to you confirming what you possess, you must believe in him and support him.’ He said, ‘Do you acknowledge this and accept My binding covenant?’ They said, ‘We acknowledge it.’ He said, ‘Then bear witness, and I am with you among the witnesses.’”

Ibn ‘Abbās said: Allah never sent a prophet without taking a covenant from him that, if Muhammad were sent while he was still alive, he would believe in him and support him. He also commanded him to take a covenant from his people that, if Muhammad were sent while they were still alive, they would believe in him and support him.

Allah Most High also said:

“And We have revealed to you the Scripture in truth, confirming the Scripture that came before it and standing as a guardian over it. So judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their desires, turning away from the truth that has come to you. To each of you We have prescribed a law and a way.”

He made belief in any of the messengers inseparable from belief in the others, and declared anyone who claimed to believe in some and disbelieve in others to be a disbeliever.

Allah Most High said:

“Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers, wish to make a distinction between Allah and His messengers, say, ‘We believe in some and disbelieve in others,’ and wish to take a path in between—it is they who are truly disbelievers.”

He also said:

“Do you then believe in part of the Scripture and disbelieve in part? What recompense is there for those among you who do this except disgrace in the life of this world? On the Day of Resurrection, they will be returned to the severest punishment.”

Through to His words: “you do.”

He has also said to us:

“Say, ‘We believe in Allah, in what has been revealed to us, in what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes, in what Moses and Jesus were given, and in what the prophets were given by their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we submit.’

“If they believe as you have believed, they are rightly guided; but if they turn away, they are only in opposition. Allah will suffice you against them, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.”

Thus, He commanded us to say: We believe in all of this, and to Him we submit. Whoever receives the message of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, but does not acknowledge what he brought is neither a Muslim nor a believer. Rather, he is a disbeliever, even if he claims to be a Muslim or a believer.

As they relate, when Allah Most High revealed:

“Whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will never be accepted from him, and in the Hereafter he will be among the losers,”

the Jews and Christians said, “We too are Muslims.” Then Allah revealed:

“Pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to Allah by people who are able to make their way there.”

They said, “We will not perform pilgrimage.” Then He, Most High, said:

“Whoever disbelieves—Allah has no need of any of His creation.”

For submission to Allah is not complete without acknowledging His right over His servants to require pilgrimage to the House, just as

he, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Islam is built upon five: testifying that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establishing prayer, giving zakāh, fasting Ramadan, and performing pilgrimage to the House.”

Thus, when the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, stood at ʿArafah, Allah Most High revealed:

“Today I have perfected your religion for you, completed My favour upon you, and chosen Islam as your religion.”

People have disputed whether the earlier followers of Moses and Jesus were Muslims. “This is a dispute over terminology.” Islam in the specific sense—the religion with which Allah sent Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, encompassing the law of the Quran—is followed only by the community of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him. Today, when used without qualification, “Islam” refers to this. Islam in the general sense, however, encompasses every law with which Allah sent a prophet, and thus includes the submission of every community that followed one of the prophets.

The foundation of Islam in every sense is the testimony that there is no god but Allah. All the messengers were sent with this, as Allah Most High said:

“We certainly sent a messenger to every nation, saying, ‘Worship Allah and shun tāghūt.’”

Allah Most High also said:

“We never sent a messenger before you without revealing to him: ‘There is no god but Me, so worship Me.’”

He said of His intimate friend, Abraham:

“And when Abraham said to his father and his people, ‘I am free of all that you worship, except the One who created me; He will surely guide me.’ And he made this an enduring declaration among his descendants, so that they might return.”

Allah Most High also related his words:

“Have you considered what you have been worshipping—you and your forefathers? They are enemies to me, except the Lord of all worlds.”

Allah Most High said:

“You have a good example in Abraham and those with him, when they said to their people, ‘We are free of you and whatever you worship besides Allah. We reject you, and there has arisen between us and you

enmity and hatred forever, until you believe in Allah.’” He also said:

“And ask the messengers We sent before you: did We appoint gods besides the Most Merciful to be worshipped?”

He related that His messengers, such as Noah, Hūd, Sālih, and others, said to their people:

“Worship Allah; you have no god other than Him.”

He said of the People of the Cave:

“They were young men who believed in their Lord, and We increased them in guidance. We strengthened their hearts when they stood up and said, ‘Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. We will never invoke any god besides Him, for then we would have said something far removed from the truth.’”

The passage continues to His words:

“Who, then, is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah?”

He, glorified be He, also said:

“Indeed, Allah does not forgive associating partners with Him, but He forgives anything less than that for whomever He wills.”

He stated this in two places in His Book. In His Book, He also explained the association of angels, prophets, celestial bodies, and idols with Allah—and the root of all such association is associating Satan with Him. He said of the Christians:

“They took their scholars and monks as lords besides Allah, and also the Messiah, son of Mary, although they were commanded only to worship one God. There is no god but Him. Glory be to Him, far above whatever they associate with Him.”

Allah Most High said:

“And when Allah said, ‘O Jesus, son of Mary, did you tell people, “Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah”?’ He said, ‘Glory be to You! It is not for me to say what I have no right to say. “Nor would he command you to take the angels and prophets as lords. Would he command you to disbelief after you have become Muslims?”

He thus made clear that taking the angels and prophets as lords constitutes disbelief. It is well known that no created being has claimed that the prophets, scholars, monks, or the Messiah, son of Mary, shared with Allah in creating the heavens and the earth. Indeed, no one has even claimed that the world has two makers equal in their attributes and actions.

Nor has any descendant of Adam affirmed the existence of a god equal to Allah in all His attributes. Rather, most of those who associate partners with Allah acknowledge that the partner they associate with Him is not His equal. Indeed, most acknowledge that this partner belongs to Him, whether it is an angel, a prophet, a celestial body, or an idol. Thus, the Arab polytheists used to say in their pilgrimage invocation:

“Here I am at Your service. You have no partner except a partner who belongs to You: You own him and whatever he owns.”

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, raised his voice proclaiming Allah’s oneness, saying:

“Here I am at Your service, O Allah, here I am. Here I am; You have no partner; here I am. Indeed, all praise and blessings are Yours, as is sovereignty. You have no partner.”

The writers on religious doctrines have recorded what they collected of the views of earlier and later peoples concerning religions, sects, opinions, and beliefs. Yet they have not reported anyone affirming a partner who shares with Him in creating all created things, or an equal to Him in all His attributes. Rather, among the most significant

views they have recorded on this subject is that of the dualists, who affirm two principles, “light” and “darkness,” and hold that light created good and darkness created evil. They then report two views held by them concerning darkness. The first is that it came into being, in which case it is among the things created by light. The second is that it is without beginning, but has produced only evil, and is therefore inferior to light in its essence, its attributes, and what it produces.

He, glorified be He, has told us in His Book of the polytheists’ acknowledgment that Allah is the Creator of all created things. He says:

“If you ask them who created the heavens and the earth, they will surely say, ‘Allah.’ Say, ‘Have you considered those you invoke besides Allah? If Allah intended harm for me, could they remove that harm? Or if He intended mercy for me, could they withhold His mercy?’ Say, ‘Allah is sufficient for me. In Him do those who trust put their trust.’”

And He, exalted be He, says:

“Say, ‘To whom belong the earth and whoever is in it, if you know?’”

“Say, ‘Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Mighty Throne?’”

“They will say, ‘To Allah.’ Say, ‘Will you not then fear Him?’”

The passage continues to His words:

“How, then, are you deluded?”

“Most of them do not believe in Allah without associating partners with Him.”

speculative theologians who expound Allah’s oneness in their books of theology and rational inquiry go no further than dividing it into (three types). They say: He is one in His essence, having no parts; one in His attributes, having no likeness; and one in His actions, having no partner.

The best-known of these three types among them is the third, namely “oneness in actions,” which means that the Creator of the world is one. They argue for this using what they call the argument of mutual hindrance and other proofs. They suppose that this is the affirmation of Allah’s oneness that is required, and that this is the meaning of our statement, “There is no god but Allah.” Indeed, they may even define divinity as the power to bring things into existence.

It is well known that the Arab polytheists to whom Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was first sent did not disagree with him on this. Rather, they acknowledged that Allah is the Creator of everything. They even acknowledged divine decree, yet remained polytheists.

It has thus become clear that no one in the world disputes the basis of this polytheism. The most that can be said, however, is that some people have held that certain existing things were created by someone other than Allah, such as the Qadariyya and others. Yet these people acknowledge that Allah created His servants and their ability, even if they say that the servants created their own actions.

Likewise, the adherents of philosophy, naturalism, and astrology who hold that some created beings bring certain things into existence, while acknowledging the Maker, regard these agents as themselves fashioned

As for anyone who denies the Maker, he rejects and denies the Maker’s existence, as in the claim Pharaoh openly professed. Our discussion here, however, concerns those who associate partners with Allah while acknowledging His existence. These polytheists do not dispute the oneness that those theologians have established. The same applies to the “second type”—their statement that “He has no likeness in His attributes.” No nation has affirmed a being without beginning equal to Him in His essence, whether it claimed that such a being acts jointly with Him or that it does not act at all. Rather, anyone who likens something of His creation to Him does so only in certain respects. Reason establishes that no created being can be His equal, sharing with Him everything that is necessary, possible, or impossible with respect to Him. That would entail affirming two contradictories at once, as discussed earlier.

Reason also establishes that any two self-subsisting beings must have something in common, such as both falling under the concepts of existence, self-subsistence, essence, and the like. Denying this entails total negation. The distinctive properties of lordship must also be affirmed. This has already been discussed.

Then the Jahmiyya, including the Muʿtazila and others, incorporated the denial of the divine attributes into what they called the affirmation of Allah’s oneness. Thus, if someone says that Allah has knowledge or power, that He will be seen in the Hereafter, or that the Quran is Allah’s speech, sent down and uncreated, they say: “He likens Allah to His creation and does not affirm His oneness.”

And the extremists among the philosophers and the Qarmatians went further, denying His most beautiful names and saying: “Whoever says that Allah is All-Knowing, All-Powerful, Almighty, and All-Wise likens Him to His creation and does not affirm His oneness.” The most extreme among these extremists went further still, saying: “He cannot be described through either negation or affirmation, because both entail likening Him to something else.”

All of them fell into a form of likening far worse than what they sought to escape: they likened Him to impossible things, nonexistent things, and inanimate objects, seeking to avoid what they claimed was likening Him to living beings. Yet it is well known that these attributes, which are affirmed for Allah, do not belong to Him in the same manner as they belong to any created being whatsoever. He—glorified and exalted is He—has nothing like Him in His essence, His attributes, or His actions. Thus, there is no difference between affirming His essence and affirming His attributes. If affirming His essence does not entail affirming its likeness to other essences, then affirming His attributes does not entail affirming any likeness to Him in those attributes. These Jahmiyya, who deny the divine attributes, therefore call this the affirmation of Allah’s oneness, describe its opposite as likening Him to His creation, and call themselves those who affirm His oneness.

The same applies to the “third type,” namely their statement: “He is one, with no division in His essence,” or “He has no part,” or “He has no portion.” This wording is ambiguous. For Allah—glorified is He—is “One, the Eternal Refuge. He neither begets nor is born, and there is none equal to Him.” It is therefore impossible for Him to be divided, to be broken into parts, or to have been composed of parts. Yet they include within this wording the denial that He is above His Throne, separate from His creation, and distinct from them, along with other such meanings that entail negating Him and denying His attributes. They count this as part of affirming His oneness.

It has thus become clear that what they call the affirmation of Allah’s oneness contains both truth and falsehood. Even if it were all true, the polytheists’ acknowledgment of all of it would not free them from the polytheism with which Allah described them in the Quran and for which the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—fought them. Rather, they must acknowledge that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah.

What is meant by (a deity) is not one who has the power to bring things into existence, as some leading speculative theologians supposed. They thought that divinity meant having this power to the exclusion of all others, and that whoever acknowledged that Allah alone has the power to bring things into existence had thereby testified that there is no deity except Him. Yet the polytheists acknowledged this while remaining polytheists, as explained earlier. Rather, the true deity is the One who deserves to be worshipped. He is a deity in the sense of one who is worshipped, not one who worships. Affirming Allah’s oneness means worshipping Allah alone, without any partner; associating partners with Him means setting up another deity alongside Allah.

And if it becomes clear that the utmost these speculative thinkers establish—those who affirm divine decree and identify themselves with the Sunnah—is merely Allah’s oneness in His lordship, and that Allah is the Lord of everything, even though the polytheists acknowledged this while remaining polytheists, then the same applies to certain groups of Sufis and those who profess spiritual knowledge, realization, and the affirmation of Allah’s oneness. deny divine decree. Although they attach great importance to the commands and prohibitions, the promise of reward and the threat of punishment—and go to excess in this—they deny divine decree and thus have an element of associating partners with Allah in this respect.

Acknowledging the commands and prohibitions, the promise of reward and the threat of punishment while denying divine decree is better than acknowledging divine decree while denying the commands and prohibitions, the promise of reward and the threat of punishment. Hence, during the time of the Companions and the Successors, there was no one who denied these commands, prohibitions, promises, and threats, although the Qadariyya had emerged among them, as had the Khawārij—the Harūriyya. The religious innovations that first appear are those whose error is less apparent. The weaker those who uphold the light of prophethood become, the stronger religious innovation grows.

Thus, these Sufis who witness the reality of Allah’s universal lordship while disregarding His commands and prohibitions are worse than the Qadariyya of the Mu'tazila and others like them. The latter resemble the Magians, whereas these Sufis resemble the polytheists who said:

“If Allah had willed, we would not have associated partners with Him, nor would our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything.”

The polytheists are worse than the Magians. This, then, is a momentous principle that every Muslim must understand, for it is the foundation of Islam by which the basis of faith is distinguished from what the unbelievers follow: belief in Allah’s oneness and in His Messenger’s mission, expressed in the testimony that none is worthy of worship except Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.

Many people have failed to uphold the true meaning of these two foundations, or one of them, while imagining that they have attained the utmost realization of truth, monotheism, knowledge, and spiritual understanding.

Thus, a polytheist’s acknowledgment that Allah is the Lord, Sovereign, and Creator of all things does not save him from Allah’s punishment unless it is accompanied by his acknowledgment that none is worthy of worship except Allah—so no one but Him deserves worship—and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, whose reports must therefore be believed and whose commands must be obeyed. These two foundations must therefore be discussed.

The First Foundation: “Allah’s Oneness in Worship”

As noted earlier, Allah, glorified is He, has told us that the polytheists established intermediaries between themselves and Allah, invoking them and taking them as intercessors without Allah’s permission. Allah Most High says:

“They worship besides Allah what can neither harm nor benefit them, and say, ‘These are our intercessors with Allah.’ Say, ‘Are you informing Allah of something He does not know in the heavens or on earth?’ Glorified and exalted is He above what they associate with Him!”

He thus declares that those who took these beings as intercessors are polytheists. Allah Most High also relates the words of the believer mentioned in Surah Yā-Sīn:

“Why should I not worship the One who created me, and to whom you will be returned?

“Should I take gods besides Him? If the Most Merciful intends any harm for me, their intercession will avail me nothing, nor can they rescue me.

“I would then surely be in manifest error.

“I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me.”

Allah Most High says:

“You have come to Us alone, just as We created you the first time, leaving behind all that We bestowed upon you. We do not see with you your intercessors, whom you claimed to be partners in your affairs. The bonds between you have been severed, and those you used to claim have forsaken you.”

He, glorified is He, thus tells us that they claimed their intercessors to be partners in their affairs. Allah Most High says:

“Have they taken intercessors besides Allah? Say, ‘Even though they possess nothing and have no understanding?’

“Say, ‘All intercession belongs to Allah. His is the dominion of the heavens and the earth. Then to Him you will be returned.’”

Allah Most High says: “You have no

protector or intercessor besides Him.” Allah Most High says:

“And warn with it those who fear being gathered before their Lord, for they will have no protector or intercessor besides Him.”

Allah Most High says:

“Who can intercede with Him except by His permission?”

Allah Most High says:

“They say, ‘The Most Merciful has taken a son.’ Glory be to Him! Rather, they are honored servants.

“They do not speak before He does, and they act at His command.

“He knows what lies before them and what lies behind them. They intercede only for those with whom He is pleased, and they tremble in awe of Him.”

Allah Most High says:

“How many angels there are in the heavens whose intercession avails nothing unless Allah first grants permission for whomever He wills and is pleased with.”

Allah Most High says:

“Say, ‘Call upon those whom you claim besides Allah. They possess not even an atom’s weight in the heavens or on earth. They have no share in either, nor does He have any helper among them.’

“Intercession with Him is of no benefit except for one to whom He grants permission.”

Allah Most High says:

“Say, ‘Call upon those whom you claim besides Him. They have no power to remove your affliction or to shift it elsewhere.’

“Those whom they invoke themselves seek a means of drawing near to their Lord, striving to be closest to Him. They hope for His mercy and fear His punishment. Surely your Lord’s punishment is to be feared.”

A group of the early generations said: Some people used to invoke Ezra, the Messiah, and the angels. Allah therefore revealed this verse, explaining that the angels and prophets seek to draw near to Allah, hope for His mercy, and fear His punishment.

Truly upholding Allah’s oneness includes knowing that Allah Most High has established for Himself a right in which no created being shares, such as worship, reliance, fear, reverent awe, and God-consciousness. As Allah Most High says:

“Do not set up another god alongside Allah, lest you be left condemned and forsaken.”

Allah Most High says: “Indeed, We have sent down

to you the Book in truth, so worship Allah, devoting your religion sincerely to Him.” Allah Most High says:

“Say, ‘I have been commanded to worship Allah, devoting my religion sincerely to Him.’”

Allah Most High says:

“Say, ‘Is it other than Allah that you command me to worship, O ignorant ones?’”

Through to His words: “the grateful.”

Each messenger says to his people:

“Worship Allah; you have no god other than Him.”

Regarding reliance, Allah Most High says:

“And put your trust in Allah, if you are believers.”

“And in Allah let the believers put their trust.”

He says:

“Say, ‘Allah is sufficient for me. In Him those who trust put their trust.’”

Allah Most High says:

“Had they been content with what Allah and His Messenger gave them, and said, ‘Allah is sufficient for us. Allah will give us of His bounty, and so will His Messenger. To Allah we turn with longing.’”

Thus, regarding giving, He says: “what Allah and His Messenger gave them.” But regarding reliance, He says: “and said, ‘Allah is sufficient for us,’” without adding “and His Messenger.” For giving here means giving in accordance with revealed law. This includes the permissions and declarations of lawfulness conveyed by the Messenger: what is lawful is what he has declared lawful, what is unlawful is what he has forbidden, and religion is what he has prescribed. Allah Most High says:

“Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it.”

As for being sufficient, this means being enough; Allah alone suffices His servant. As Allah Most High says:

“Those to whom people said, ‘The people have gathered against you, so fear them,’ but this only increased them in faith, and they said, ‘Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.’”

He alone is sufficient for them all. Allah Most High says:

“O Prophet, Allah is sufficient for you and for the believers who follow you.”

That is, Allah is sufficient for you and for those believers who follow you: He suffices for you all.

And it does not mean that Allah and the believers together are sufficient for you, as some mistakenly suppose. He alone suffices His Prophet; He is sufficient for him, and no one shares with Him in sufficing the Messenger. This linguistic construction is like the poet’s words:

“A sword of Indian steel suffices for you and al-Dahhāk.”

The Arabs also say: “A dirham suffices for you and Zayd,” meaning that one dirham suffices for both of you.

Regarding fear, reverent awe, and mindfulness of Allah, He says:

“Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, fears Allah and is mindful of Him—it is they who will triumph.”

Thus, He affirms obedience to both Allah and the Messenger, but reserves reverent awe and mindfulness for Allah alone. Likewise, Noah, peace be upon him, said:

“Indeed, I am a clear warner to you.”

“Worship Allah, be mindful of Him, and obey me.”

He therefore directs worship and mindfulness to Allah alone, and obedience to the Messenger; for whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah.

Allah Most High says:

“So do not fear people, but fear Me.”

Allah Most High also says:

“So do not fear them, but fear Me, if you are believers.”

Abraham, the close friend of Allah, peace be upon him, said:

“How could I fear what you associate with Allah, while you do not fear associating with Allah that for which He has sent down no authority to you? Which of the two parties has more right to security, if you know?”

“Those who believe and do not mix their faith with wrongdoing—it is they who will have security, and they are rightly guided.”

In the two Sahīh collections, Ibn Masʿūd is reported to have said: When this verse was revealed, it troubled the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and they said: “Which of us has not wronged himself?”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, replied:

“It refers only to associating partners with Allah. Have you not heard the words of the righteous servant: ‘Indeed, associating partners with Allah is a tremendous wrong’?”

Allah Most High says:

“So fear Me alone.”

“And be mindful of Me alone.”

Another example of this is that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would say in his sermons:

“Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger is rightly guided. Whoever disobeys them harms only himself and will not harm Allah in the least.”

He also said:

“And do not say, ‘What Allah wills and Muhammad wills,’ but say, ‘What Allah wills, then what Muhammad wills.’”

Thus, when speaking of obedience, he joined the Messenger’s name to Allah’s with the conjunction “and”; but when speaking of the will, he instructed that “then” be used. This is because obedience to the Messenger is obedience to Allah: whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah, and obedience to Allah is obedience to the Messenger. The will, however, is different: no servant’s will is Allah’s will, nor does Allah’s will necessarily entail the will of His servants. Rather, whatever Allah wills happens, even if people do not will it; and whatever people will does not happen unless Allah wills it.

The Second Principle: The Rights of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace

We must therefore believe in him, obey him, follow him, please him, love him, submit to his judgment, and the like

thereof. Allah Most High says:

“Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Allah and His Messenger are more worthy of being pleased.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Say: If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your spouses, your relatives, the wealth you have acquired, the trade whose decline you fear, and the homes you cherish are dearer to you than Allah, His Messenger, and striving in His cause, then wait until Allah brings about His command.”

Allah Most High also says:

“But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge concerning the disputes that arise among them, then find within themselves no discomfort over what you have decided and submit completely.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Say: If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you.”

And there are other similar passages.

Section

Once this is established, it is well known that one must believe in Allah’s creation and command: in His decree and His revealed law.

The misguided who delve into divine decree have divided into three groups: the Magian group, the polytheistic group, and the followers of Iblīs.

The Magian group consists of those who deny Allah’s decree, even though they believe in His commands and prohibitions. Their extremists deny His foreknowledge and the written decree, while their less extreme adherents deny the all-encompassing scope of His will, creation, and power. These are the Muʿtazilah and those who agree with them.

The second group, the polytheistic group, consists of those who acknowledge divine ordainment and decree but deny commands and prohibitions. Allah Most High says:

“Those who associate others with Allah will say, ‘If Allah had willed, neither we nor our fathers would have associated others with Him, nor would we have forbidden anything.’”

Whoever invokes divine decree to justify setting aside commands and prohibitions belongs to this group. This has become widespread among those Sufis who claim to have attained spiritual reality.

The third group, the followers of Iblīs, consists of those who acknowledge both, but regard them as a contradiction on the part of the Lord—glorified and exalted is He—and impugn His wisdom and justice. Such views are related of Iblīs, their leader, as recorded by writers on sectarian doctrines and transmitted from the People of the Book.

The point is that these are fabrications of those who have gone astray. As for those who are guided and attain success, they believe in both. They believe that Allah is the Creator, Lord, and Sovereign of everything; that whatever He wills comes to pass, and whatever He does not will does not come to pass; that He has power over all things, encompasses everything in His knowledge, and has recorded everything in a clear Record. This principle affirms Allah’s knowledge, power, will, oneness, and lordship, and that He is the Creator, Lord, and Sovereign of everything—all of which are fundamental principles of faith.

Yet they do not deny the causes Allah has created, through which He creates their effects. As He Most High says:

“Until, when they carry heavy clouds, We drive them to a lifeless land, then send down water through it, and with that water bring forth fruits of every kind.”

And He Most High says:

“Through it Allah guides those who follow what pleases Him to the ways of peace.”

And He Most High says:

“He causes many to go astray through it, and guides many through it.”

He thus tells us that He acts through causes. Whoever says that He acts when they occur, but not through them, contradicts what the Quran teaches and denies the powers and natural properties Allah has created. This is akin to denying the powers Allah has created in living beings, through which they act, such as a human being’s capacity to act. Likewise, whoever regards these powers as themselves the creators of those effects has associated partners with Allah and attributed His action to another.

For every cause depends upon another cause for its effect to occur. There must also be an impediment that prevents it from producing its effect unless Allah removes that impediment. Thus, there is nothing in

existence that can bring anything about independently whenever it wills, except Allah alone. He Most High says:

“And of everything We have created pairs, so that you may take heed.”

That is, so that you may know that the Creator of all pairs is One. Thus, anyone who says, “Only one thing can proceed from Allah, because only one thing can proceed from the One,” is ignorant. For there is no single being in existence that has produced anything by itself—neither one thing nor two—except Allah, who created all pairs: of what the earth grows, of themselves, and of things they do not know.

Fire, in which Allah has created heat, only causes burning when there is both fire and something susceptible to being burned. If it falls upon a salamander, a ruby, or something similar, it does not burn them. A body may also be coated with something that prevents it from burning. Likewise, the rays emitted by the sun require a body upon which they can be reflected. If a barrier, such as a cloud or a roof, intervenes, the rays do not reach beneath it. This has been explained at length elsewhere.

The point here is that “belief in divine decree” is indispensable, for belief in divine decree completes belief in Allah’s oneness. As Ibn ‘Abbās said: “It is what holds belief in Allah’s oneness together. Whoever affirms Allah’s oneness and believes in divine decree has perfected his belief in His oneness; whoever affirms Allah’s oneness but denies divine decree has undone his belief in His oneness.”

Belief in the revealed law is also indispensable: belief in the commands and prohibitions, the promises and warnings, with which Allah sent His messengers and revealed His Books.

And human beings cannot do without a law to live by in this world, for they must act to secure benefit and act to ward off harm. The revealed law distinguishes between actions that benefit them and actions that harm them. It is Allah’s justice within His creation and His light among His servants. Human beings therefore cannot live without a law by which they distinguish what they should do from what they should refrain from doing.

What is meant by law is not merely justice between people in their dealings. Even a person living alone must do some things and refrain from others, for a human being is one who continually intends and acts. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The names that most truthfully describe their bearers are Hārith and Hammām.”

This is what is meant by describing a human being as acting through volition. When someone has a will, he acts upon it, and he must know whether what he wants is beneficial or harmful to him, and whether it makes him better or corrupts him.

People know some of this through their innate disposition, just as they know that eating and drinking benefit them, and just as their innate disposition gives them self-evident knowledge. Others know it through inference, as with the conclusions to which their reason guides them. Some of it, however, they know only through the messengers’ teaching, explanation, and guidance.

It is in this connection that people have debated whether the goodness and badness of actions can be known by reason, or whether actions have no goodness or badness that can be known by reason. This has been discussed at length elsewhere, and we have explained the confusion that has arisen concerning this question. They agree that whether an act is congenial or repugnant to the one who performs it can be known by reason, which means

that the agent brings about what he loves and enjoys, and what he hates and what harms him. This much may be known through reason, through the revealed law, or through both together.

However, detailed knowledge of this, and knowledge of the ultimate outcome of actions—happiness or misery in the Hereafter—can be obtained only through revelation. People cannot know through their reason the details of the Last Day that the messengers have conveyed, or the detailed prescriptions of the revealed laws that they have commanded. Likewise, people cannot know through their reason the details of Allah’s names and attributes conveyed by the messengers, although they may know their general outlines through reason. This detailed knowledge, through which faith is attained and which the Book has brought, is indicated by the words of the Most High:

“And thus We have revealed to you an inspiration by Our command. You did not know what the Book was, nor what faith was, but We made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants.”

And His words:

“Say, ‘If I go astray, I go astray only to my own detriment; but if I am guided, it is through what my Lord reveals to me. Indeed, He is All-Hearing, Near.’”

And His words:

“Say, ‘I warn you only through revelation.’”

Yet one group mistakenly supposed that goodness and badness had a meaning other than this, and that this meaning could be known through reason. Opposing them was another group, who supposed that the goodness and badness taught by the revealed law fell outside this understanding. Both groups—those who affirmed goodness and badness as known through reason, and those who affirmed them as known through the revealed law, while excluding them from this category—were mistaken.

 وَشَبَّهُوهُ بِعِبَادِهِ فِيمَا يَأْمُرُ بِهِ وَيَنْهَى عَنْهُ فَمَنْ نَظَرَ إلَى الْقَدَرِ فَقَطْ وَعَظَّمَ الْفَنَاءَ فِي تَوْحِيدِ الرُّبُوبِيَّةِ وَوَقَفَ عِنْدَ الْحَقِيقَةِ الْكَوْنِيَّةِ:
 لَمْ يُمَيِّزْ بَيْنَ الْعِلْمِ وَالْجَهْلِ وَالصِّدْقِ وَالْكَذِبِ وَالْبِرِّ وَالْفُجُورِ وَالْعَدْلِ وَالظُّلْمِ وَالطَّاعَةِ وَالْمَعْصِيَةِ وَالْهُدَى وَالضَّلَالِ وَالرَّشَادِ وَالْغَيِّ وَأَوْلِيَاءِ اللَّهِ وَأَعْدَائِهِ وَأَهْلِ الْجَنَّةِ وَأَهْلِ النَّارِ وَهَؤُلَاءِ مَعَ أَنَّهُمْ مُخَالِفُونَ بِالضَّرُورَةِ لِكُتُبِ اللَّهِ وَدِينِهِ وَشَرَائِعِهِ فَهُمْ
translated_text:
Moreover, since both groups denied that Allah is described as possessing love, pleasure, displeasure, joy, and similar attributes conveyed by the divine texts and supported by rational evidence, they disagreed—despite agreeing that Allah does nothing that would be bad on His part. They held two views on whether such an act is intrinsically impossible, whether it is inconceivable that He could have the power to do anything bad, and whether He—glorified be He—is above such acts and refrains from them solely because of the badness discernible by reason that they had posited.

Both views deviate in the same manner as the two views mentioned earlier. The first group drew no distinction, in His creation and command, between guidance and misguidance, obedience and disobedience, the righteous and the wicked, the people of Paradise and the people of Hell, or mercy and punishment. Thus, they did not regard Him as deserving praise for the justice He exercises or the injustice He refrains from, nor for the kindness and blessings He bestows or the torment and retribution He withholds. The other group declared Him above such acts on the basis of the badness discernible by reason that they had posited, which has no reality. They placed Him on the same footing as His creatures regarding what is good and bad, and likened Him to His servants regarding what He commands and forbids.

Whoever considers divine decree alone, extols absorption in the affirmation of Allah’s sole lordship, and stops at the reality of His governance of creation does not distinguish between knowledge and ignorance, truthfulness and falsehood, righteousness and wickedness, justice and injustice, obedience and disobedience, guidance and misguidance, right conduct and waywardness, Allah’s allies and His enemies, or the people of Paradise and the people of Hell. Although these people indisputably contradict Allah’s Books, His religion, and His revealed laws, they are

translated_text:
also at odds with the self-evident truths of sensory perception and direct experience, and of reason and inference. Each of them inevitably takes pleasure in some things and suffers pain from others. He therefore distinguishes between what he eats and drinks and what he does not, and between heat and cold that harm him and those that do not. This distinction between what benefits him and what harms him constitutes the reality of revealed law and religion.

Whoever supposes that a human being can reach a point at which these two are always equal to him has made a false claim and contradicted the self-evident evidence of the senses. A person may, however, occasionally experience a condition such as intoxication, unconsciousness, or something similar that prevents him from perceiving certain things. But for his perception to cease entirely while he remains alive is impossible. Even a sleeping person has not lost his own awareness: in his dreams he sometimes sees things that distress him and at other times things that delight him.

Thus, the states described as overwhelming absorption, self-effacement, intoxication, and the like involve only a lack of awareness of some things rather than others. Although they reflect a deficiency in the person experiencing them—because his discernment is impaired—they never reach a point at which discernment disappears altogether. Whoever denies all discernment in this spiritual station and exalts it has misunderstood both the reality of creation and the reality of religion: divine decree and revealed law. He has misunderstood Allah’s creation and His command, supposing that such a state exists when it has no existence, and supposing it to be praiseworthy when there is nothing praiseworthy in lacking discernment—that is, reason and knowledge.
